conflicts.issue: Approval vs. Delay of Made in Durham Youth Program Contract Modification (Item 18)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 5-2 over whether to immediately authorize the Made in Durham contract modification or delay action to allow further review of a resident's critique of the organization's service model and internship outcomes.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the contract modification immediately to avoid financial hardship on an ongoing workforce partnership.
side_a_arguments: The contract period began July 1 and Made in Durham's work-based collaborative supporting 600 Durham YouthWorks internships had already launched.
Staff and the City Manager warned delaying approval would create financial hardship for the organization and noted the item had already gone through the regular work session review.
conflicts.side_b_position: Delay consideration of the contract modification to examine community concerns about outcomes and target youth reach.
side_b_arguments: A resident asked for additional time to review materials regarding Made in Durham's deviation from its original service model and limited internship yield relative to applicants.
Concerns were raised about whether the students being served matched the initial equity and program criteria.
conflicts.resolution: Motion to execute the contract modification passed 5-2; Charlie Reece noted after the vote that he supported the contract itself and voted No solely to represent the resident's request for a delay.

conflicts.issue: Approval vs. Delay of Made in Durham Youth Program Contract Modification (Item 18)
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-2 over whether to approve the Made in Durham youth program contract modification immediately or delay the vote to examine a resident's concerns about performance and target-youth reach.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the contract modification immediately to prevent financial disruption to ongoing youth workforce programming.
side_a_arguments: The contract period started July 1 and the work-based collaborative supporting Durham YouthWorks' 600-internship goal was already underway.
Delaying execution would create financial hardship for Made in Durham after the item had already passed work session review.
conflicts.side_b_position: Delay the vote to give community members and Council more time to assess service-model deviations and youth reach.
side_b_arguments: A resident requested more time to review performance materials alleging deviations from the original service model and insufficient internship yield.
DeDreana Freeman raised concerns over whether intended Black-owned businesses and target youth populations were actually being reached.
conflicts.resolution: Contract modification passed 5-2; Charlie Reece stated afterward he supported the contract and voted No solely to reflect the resident's request for a delay.

conflicts.issue: 1001 Olive Branch Road Annexation and Urban Node Rezoning
conflicts.summary: Council divided 3-4 over whether to annex and rezone 1001 Olive Branch Road near Research Triangle Park, weighing existing comprehensive plan alignment and voluntary proffers against sustainability and growth-management expectations.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support annexation and rezoning as consistent with existing precedent and RTP-adjacent growth.
side_a_arguments: Proximity to Research Triangle Park supports creating an urban node in the area.
The applicant's voluntary proffers for affordable housing and Durham Public Schools followed established precedent.
The proposal met current legal and comprehensive plan standards rather than justifying an ad hoc denial.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny annexation because the project falls short on sustainability and comprehensive plan expectations.
side_b_arguments: Even where current comprehensive plan rules allow it, developers must meet higher sustainability standards.
Approving projects that fail long-term sustainability and generational stewardship principles prevents better development outcomes.
Any urban node in this corridor needs to be planned properly before extending city annexation.
conflicts.resolution: The annexation ordinance failed 3-4, ending consideration of the companion rezoning.

conflicts.issue: Carrington Woods (833 Clayton Road) Consolidated Annexation and RS-10 Rezoning Without a Development Plan
conflicts.summary: Council split 3-4 on annexing and rezoning 8.57 acres near Southern High School from RS-20 to RS-10 without a binding development plan, dividing over neighborhood traffic/pedestrian safety concerns, developer accountability, and whether to delay for additional information.
conflicts.side_a_position: Hold the hearing open or approve the annexation/RS-10 rezoning because the modest density increase creates minimal additional traffic beyond by-right development.
side_a_arguments: Transportation staff reported adjacent roads operate below LOS D only in brief 30-minute school rush-hour windows, and adding 7 to 16 lots over by-right RS-20 would not materially worsen traffic.
Holding the public hearing open could let the absent applicant return to provide non-binding assurances on lot count.
conflicts.side_b_position: Decide the case immediately and reject annexation/RS-10 rezoning due to lack of a binding development plan, pedestrian safety gaps, and unequal community treatment.
side_b_arguments: After the Planning Commission delayed two months and voted 2-11 against the project, the applicant still refused to file a development plan locking in lot counts.

Neighborhood residents should not be forced to return a fourth time, and lower-income areas near Southern High School deserve the same developer engagement expected in affluent neighborhoods like Forest Hills.
Unmitigated pedestrian and bus-stop safety gaps along Clayton Road remain unaddressed.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation failed 3-4 at 02:34:30, halting the rezoning.

conflicts.issue: Tax-Exempt Conduit Bond Approval for Excelsior Classical Academy Charter School (Item 23)
conflicts.summary: Council split 2-5 on approving a TEFRA resolution enabling Excelsior Classical Academy to issue up to $20 million in tax-exempt conduit bonds via Wisconsin's Public Finance Authority.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the conduit bond resolution because the City bears no financial liability and denying tax-exempt refinancing penalizes Durham students already attending the school.
side_a_arguments: The school already holds a state charter and owns the building on an interim loan; denying tax-exempt bonds will not prevent expansion and only forces taxable debt that pulls operating funds away from students.
Municipal TEFRA hearings should not be used as a philosophical foil against charter schools when the City contributes zero public dollars and has no jurisdiction over education policy.
Withholding financing leaves the school more financially vulnerable to outside management lender TeamCFA.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny the conduit bond resolution because the City should exercise its discretion not to lend a municipal financing tool to charter school expansion.
side_b_arguments: Charter school expansion diverts per-pupil tax dollars and families away from Durham Public Schools, which serve the majority of low-income and Black and brown students.
Excelsior has ongoing financial ties (forgivable loans and a voting board seat) to TeamCFA, whose state takeover politics threaten local public schools.
The school has alternative taxable or governmental financing options without Durham City Council's official stamp of approval.
conflicts.resolution: Motion failed 2-5 at 01:16:26.

conflicts.issue: Participatory Budgeting (PB) Guidelines and Ward-Based Process
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-2 on adopting PB guidelines that initially organized the process by Durham's three wards, with Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman objecting to process transparency, racial equity safeguards, and ward structure.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt the committee-crafted PB guidelines with flexibility to adjust ward boundaries after year one
side_a_arguments: Guidelines reflected extensive work-session compromise led by Javiera Caballero, Vernetta Alston, and DeDreana Freeman
Removing 'only' from the first-year ward clause prevented boxing Council into an immediate guideline amendment while keeping the launch on schedule
conflicts.side_b_position: Delay or revise the guidelines to fix structural ward inequities, transparency, and racial equity criteria before launching
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton objected to proceeding with ward boundaries that colleagues already acknowledged were structurally problematic just to meet a timeline
DeDreana Freeman argued the process lacked clear racial equity benchmarks and adequate outreach to Black and low-income communities
conflicts.resolution: PB guidelines passed 5-2.

conflicts.issue: Participatory Budgeting FY 2020 Funding Amount ($2.4M vs. $750K–$1M)
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-2 over how much FY 2019-20 capital/project funding to commit to participatory budgeting, pitting a $2.4 million coalition against fiscal incrementalism favored by Mark-Anthony Middleton ($750,000) and Steve Schewel ($1 million).
conflicts.side_a_position: Allocate $2.4 million ($800,000 per ward) to make PB projects meaningful and drive broad resident participation
side_a_arguments: Jillian Johnson cited the national best practice of $1M per 100,000 residents and strong fund balance reserves that avoid tax hikes
Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, and Vernetta Alston argued a substantial pot enables residents—including non-voters—to propose impactful neighborhood projects
DeDreana Freeman voted Yes while pledging strict vigilance on racial equity and people-of-color representation
conflicts.side_b_position: Start with the staff-recommended $750,000 (Middleton) or at most $1 million (Schewel) in year one and scale up later
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton urged incrementalism aligned with staff's $750,000 recommendation so more dollars stay focused on housing eviction diversion, jobs, and justice-involved residents
Steve Schewel supported PB strongly but considered $1 million sufficient for a first-year pilot before scaling
conflicts.resolution: Motion allocating $2.4 million for FY 2019-20 PB projects passed 5-2.

conflicts.issue: Rescinding 2010 Petitioned Water Mains on Bandock/Rondelay Drive and Olive Branch/Bookman Street
conflicts.summary: Council divided 4-3 on rescinding two 2010 petitioned water mains outside city limits, weighing cost and future annexation/sewer plans against residents' fire-safety concerns and Olive Branch Baptist Church's failing well.
conflicts.side_a_position: Rescind the old petitioned water main orders per Public Works recommendation
side_a_arguments: Bandock/Rondelay residents already receive water from Aqua and could pursue annexation in roughly four years when a regional sewer pump station is completed
Rescinding avoids high city construction costs under outdated 2010 petition rates
conflicts.side_b_position: Vote against rescinding and honor the 2010 utility orders
side_b_arguments: Residents on Bandock/Rondelay cited lack of fire hydrants and fire protection, and Olive Branch Baptist Church reported a failing well and offered voluntary annexation and right-of-way dedication
conflicts.resolution: Both rescission resolutions passed 4-3.

conflicts.issue: Rescinding Long-Pending Petitioned Water Mains on Stallings Road (Items 17 and 18)
conflicts.summary: Council split 3-4 against rescinding two petitioned water mains on Stallings Road after resident Teresa Price testified she had paid $6,000 in assessments, granted an easement, and waited 11 years under the 2007 petition.
conflicts.side_a_position: Rescind the old petitioned water main orders in favor of updated utility-extension policy
side_a_arguments: Staff recommended rescinding old petitions because construction costs had risen far above 2007/2010 estimates and updated policy favors residents/developers paying full cost directly
conflicts.side_b_position: Defeat rescission and honor the city's prior commitment to Stallings Road residents
side_b_arguments: Resident Teresa Price followed the city's due process in 2007, granted a temporary easement, paid assessments, and had a lien placed on her home during an 11-year city delay
A majority of Council voted against rescinding so the previously ordered water main projects would proceed under Option 1
conflicts.resolution: Both motions to rescind failed 3-4, keeping the Stallings Road water main projects active.

conflicts.issue: Rescinding 2007/Previously Ordered Sewer Mains on Red Coach/Grand Oaks and East Geer Street (Items 27 and 28)
conflicts.summary: Council split 2-4 to reject staff's recommendations to rescind previously ordered sewer mains for Red Coach/Grand Oaks Roads and East Geer Street, prioritizing the city's 2007 moral commitment and public health over staff's cost concerns.
conflicts.side_a_position: Rescind the old petitioned sewer main orders
side_a_arguments: Staff noted the 2007 resolution had no set timeline, was not a binding legal obligation, and faced steep cost escalation
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject rescission and fulfill the city's 2007 sewer commitment to residents
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton and Charlie Reece emphasized the city had a moral obligation after a decade of delay while raw sewage and failing septic systems threatened residents and creeks
NC Utilities Commission Public Staff and residents urged moving forward to solve a looming environmental problem and add sewer customers
conflicts.resolution: Both rescission motions failed 2-4, keeping the Red Coach/Grand Oaks and East Geer Street sewer projects active.

conflicts.issue: Expanding Housing Choices (EHC) UDO Text Amendment Timing, Equity Safeguards, and Displacement Risk (Item 17)
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether to immediately enact the Expanding Housing Choices UDO text amendment across all urban-tier neighborhoods or delay implementation for 12 months until the Comprehensive Plan update and stronger tenant/equity protections were in place, passing the ordinance 6-1.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt Expanding Housing Choices immediately across the urban tier (including historic districts) alongside ongoing metrics monitoring and the $95 million housing bond.
side_a_arguments: Single-family-only zoning perpetuates historical redlining and drives up prices in lower-income neighborhoods by restricting supply in high-demand areas.

Tear-downs for large luxury single-family homes are already occurring under existing rules; EHC enables incremental gentle density, small-lot homes, and ADUs that help market-rate filtering and homeowner equity.
Exempting local historic districts or delaying 12 months would perpetuate systemic inequity and stall needed housing supply after 15 months of community engagement.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose passing the amendment now without source-of-income voucher protections, unrelated-resident occupancy reforms, and waiting for the Comprehensive Plan.
side_b_arguments: Waiting 12 months for the Comprehensive Plan update would allow broader alignment rather than rushing a complex zoning overhaul.
The proposal lacks protections against Section 8 source-of-income discrimination and omits reforms to the three-unrelated-residents occupancy limit.
Removing single-family zoning without direct equity investments risks speculative developer activity in historic middle-class neighborhoods of color without guaranteeing affordable units.
conflicts.resolution: Both the consistency statement and EHC UDO text amendment passed 6-1 (DeDreana Freeman voting No), followed by a unanimous 7-0 vote on the metrics monitoring resolution.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Sept 3, 2019 (with closed captions)
conflicts.issue: Expanding Housing Choices (EHC) UDO Text Amendment Timing, Equity Safeguards, and Displacement Risk (Item 17)
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether to enact Expanding Housing Choices immediately across the urban tier or delay implementation 12 months pending the Comprehensive Plan and stronger equity/tenant protections, adopting the ordinance 6-1.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt Expanding Housing Choices immediately across urban-tier districts (including historic districts) paired with monitoring and the $95 million housing bond.
side_a_arguments: Single-family zoning reflects historical redlining and pushes displacement into lower-income neighborhoods.
Gentle infill housing choices (duplexes, ADUs, small lots) slow price escalation and support small homeowners and developers.
Delaying 12 months or exempting historic districts would perpetuate systemic inequity after 15 months of public engagement.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose immediate passage without source-of-income voucher protections, unrelated-occupant rule changes, and Comprehensive Plan integration.
side_b_arguments: The ordinance moves ahead of the Comprehensive Plan update without binding affordable housing or source-of-income protections.
Reforms to the unrelated-residents limit and anti-displacement investments should be addressed before opening neighborhoods to speculative development.
conflicts.resolution: Consistency statement and UDO text amendment passed 6-1 (DeDreana Freeman voting No), while the monitoring metrics resolution passed 7-0.

conflicts.issue: Police Officer Staffing (18 or 9 Sworn Officers) vs. Living Wage and Non-Policing Priorities in FY 2019-20 Budget
conflicts.summary: Council divided over excluding Police Chief C.J. Davis's request for 18 new sworn officers (and declining a 9-officer compromise) in favor of funding living wages for part-time city employees and equity/housing programs without raising property taxes, passing the budget 6-1.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt the $476 million FY 2019-20 budget without adding 18 new sworn police officers, prioritizing a $15.46/hour living wage for part-time staff, low-wage full-time raises, eviction diversion, and housing/equity programs without a property tax hike.
side_a_arguments: With limited revenue tools outside property taxes that burden low-income and older homeowners, funding both 18 new officers and part-time living wages was not feasible without raising taxes.

The $60 million police budget already absorbs 15 grant-funded sworn positions and adds two latent print examiners; resources are urgently needed for living wages ($650,000), Welcome Home ($200,000), eviction diversion, and the new Office of Equity and Inclusion.

Mayor Schewel noted he had supported a 9-officer compromise for shift relief and training, while DeDreana Freeman offered a friendly amendment for 9 officers (declined by Charlie Reece under single-motion rules) before joining the 6-vote majority.
conflicts.side_b_position: Vote No on the budget to protest omitting new patrol officers requested by Chief Davis and residents in high-gun-violence neighborhoods.
side_b_arguments: Over-policing stems from posture and leadership rather than headcount; proactive staffing is what maintains positive safety metrics.

Denying police staffing in high-crime communities like Cornwallis Road, Oxford Manor, and McDougald Terrace reflects a 'pecking order' in progressive politics that ignores vulnerable residents' pleas.
conflicts.resolution: Friendly amendment for 9 officers was declined by mover Charlie Reece; the FY 2019-20 budget and CIP passed 6-1 with Mark-Anthony Middleton voting No.

conflicts.issue: $95 Million Affordable Housing General Obligation Bond Order and Referendum (Item 27)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 on both the bond order and referendum resolution to place a $95 million Affordable Housing General Obligation Bond on the November 5, 2019 ballot, with DeDreana Freeman casting the sole No vote.
conflicts.side_a_position: Place the $95 million Affordable Housing Bond on the November 2019 ballot to fund thousands of affordable units, DHA redevelopment, eviction diversion, and homelessness prevention.
side_a_arguments: Routine annual operating funds cannot overcome market-driven gentrification and displacement.
The bond leverages Durham's tax base at an estimated 1.2-cent average variable (or 1.6-cent fixed) tax rate to build lasting nonprofit and Durham Housing Authority capacity.
conflicts.side_b_position: Vote No on the $95 million bond order and November referendum resolution.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman recorded No votes on both the bond order and special referendum resolution without delivering floor remarks explaining her dissent (following public comment concerns from Victoria Peterson seeking written affordability definitions and senior housing guarantees).
conflicts.resolution: Both the bond order and referendum resolution passed 6-1, with DeDreana Freeman voting No.

conflicts.issue: Timing and Displacement Risks of $95 Million General Obligation Bond Referendum (Item 15)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 to advance procedural Local Government Commission filings for the $95 million General Obligation bond referendum, with DeDreana Freeman urging a one-year delay to protect fixed-income and public-housing residents.
conflicts.side_a_position: Advance the $95 million GO bond LGC filings on the current schedule.
side_a_arguments: Proceeding with notice of intent and LGC application keeps the $95 million bond referendum on track for the current cycle.
The bond package reflects figures outlined in the Mayor's letter to Council.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer the $95 million bond referendum until the next cycle pending anti-displacement and tax-relief measures.
side_b_arguments: Advancing the bond alongside other cost and rate increases creates financial strain for fixed-income residents without clear relief levers.
An economic development plan should be established before moving forward.
Federal housing authority desegregation pushes are driving displacement of predominantly African-American housing authority residents.
conflicts.resolution: Resolutions passed 6-1, with DeDreana Freeman voting no.

conflicts.issue: 1020 Hale Street Duplex Rezoning (Item 21)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 to rezone 1020 Hale Street from RU-5 to RU-5(2) for duplexes, with DeDreana Freeman opposing both the consistency statement and UDO amendment following neighbor opposition and Planning Commission questions.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve rezoning 1020 Hale Street to RU-5(2) for duplex development.
side_a_arguments: The rezoning aligns with the Medium Density Residential designation on the future land use map.
Applicant Marty McFarling explained banks would not finance nonconforming construction or treat a single-family home with an ADU equivalently to a duplex.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose rezoning 1020 Hale Street to RU-5(2).
side_b_arguments: Opposed both the consistency statement and UDO amendment after public opposition from William Whitmore regarding rental and neighborhood impacts and Planning Commission discussion of existing single-family/ADU zoning.
conflicts.resolution: Both the consistency statement and UDO amendment passed 6-1, with DeDreana Freeman voting no.

conflicts.issue: UDO Text Amendment TC18-00006 (Private Streets Standards and County Allowance)
conflicts.summary: While six members approved TC18-00006 to clarify private street certification standards and allow an additional private-street exception primarily in Durham County, DeDreana Freeman dissented on both the consistency statement and ordinance.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the revised text amendment aligning City/County introductory standards and reflecting the County Commissioners' November 13 approval.
side_a_arguments: The applicant substantially narrowed the original proposal after the Planning Commission's 5-7 denial recommendation.
Introductory language strengthens requirements that private streets meet or exceed public street standards.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the consistency statement and UDO text amendment expanding private street allowances.
side_b_arguments: Cast Nay votes on both the consistency statement and ordinance without extended floor remarks (correcting the electronic record on the consistency vote at 02:52:25).
conflicts.resolution: Both the consistency statement and ordinance passed 6-1.

conflicts.issue: Christian Avenue Street Closing (Item 40)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 to permanently close a 331-linear-foot portion of Christian Avenue tied to the Hillsborough/Cole Mill rezoning, with DeDreana Freeman casting the sole Nay vote.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the permanent right-of-way closure as committed under approved zoning case C170030.
side_a_arguments: The closure met all UDO requirements, resolved review agency comments, and was committed as part of the prior Hillsborough/Cole Mill rezoning.
The applicant stated the segment is largely unused and would be combined with adjacent parcels.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose permanently closing the public street right-of-way.
side_b_arguments: Voted Nay without floor remarks (consistent with Freeman's broader skepticism toward vacating public rights-of-way).
conflicts.resolution: Order permanently closing Christian Avenue passed 6-1.

conflicts.issue: GoTriangle Community Engagement, Transparency, and Equity Accountability (Items 37 and 7)
conflicts.summary: Although all seven Council members ultimately supported the ROMF rezoning 7-0, DeDreana Freeman strongly criticized GoTriangle's lack of transparency, race-equity planning, and delayed disclosure of DBE and board demographic data, prompting added DBE coordination language in Item 7.
conflicts.side_a_position: Condition future GoTriangle coordination on explicit DBE utilization and hold GoTriangle accountable for race equity and transparency.
side_a_arguments: Obtaining staffing, contracting, and board diversity statistics from GoTriangle felt like 'pulling teeth' and lacked proactive environmental justice and race-equity engagement.
Neighborhood residents and communities of color bear uneven burdens from major transit infrastructure without transparent early engagement.
conflicts.side_b_position: Proceed with both the ROMF rezoning and Cooperative Agreement while acknowledging GoTriangle's recent outreach improvements and substantial minority/women workforce numbers.
side_b_arguments: John Tallmadge reported GoTriangle's workforce is 35% Black male and 31% Black female, which Mayor Schewel praised as substantial.
Light rail is a vital generational investment and Council added DBE coordination language to address Freeman's concern.
conflicts.resolution: ROMF passed 7-0; Item 7 passed with added DBE coordination language.

conflicts.issue: Boone Street and K Street Right-of-Way Closings and Encroachment Enforcement (Items 25 & 26)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 on both street closing orders (Boone Street and K Street), with DeDreana Freeman dissenting over right-of-way encroachment enforcement and utility/drainage oversight.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the permanent street closures because both met UDO standards, raised no agency objections, and retained required sewer easements.
side_a_arguments: Boone Street was an unbuilt paper street where closing legally remedies an existing driveway encroachment.
On K Street, the City retains a full sanitary sewer easement ensuring maintenance access even though Duke University's adjacent field has sat vacant.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose closing the public rights-of-way due to weak proactive enforcement against surface and underground encroachments.
side_b_arguments: Allowing unpermitted driveways and drainage/underground encroachments to be cured only retroactively via street closures reflects inadequate right-of-way patrol and enforcement.
conflicts.resolution: Both Boone Street and K Street closure orders passed 6-1.

conflicts.issue: Rolling Dale Zoning Map Change (RS-20 to PDR 3.94) and Process Ethics Concerns (Item 27)
conflicts.summary: Following a County Attorney review finding no formal ethics violation when a Planning Commissioner who voted on Rolling Dale later represented the developer, Council split 6-1 in approving the rezoning.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve PDR 3.94 rezoning on its merits despite process concerns because proffered tree buffers, setbacks, and double silt fencing protect neighbors better than by-right single-family development.
side_a_arguments: The County Attorney confirmed no county ethics violation occurred and Council could decide impartially on the merits.
Proffered 40-foot southern tree conservation, 70-foot setbacks, 34% impervious cap, and double silt fencing offer stronger protections than by-right RS-20 single-family construction.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning to PDR 3.94 and keep existing RS-20 zoning to protect waterways and neighborhood stability.
side_b_arguments: Moving from RS-20 to PDR 3.94 is a discretionary legislative action, not a by-right entitlement.
Higher density and grading pose avoidable stormwater and waterway risks to the surrounding community.
conflicts.resolution: Both the consistency statement and zoning ordinance passed 6-1.

conflicts.issue: Durham Beltline Trail Master Plan — Immediate Adoption with 90-Day Engagement Directive vs. Pause for Equity Planning (Item 28)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 to adopt the conceptual Durham Beltline Trail Master Plan while directing staff to return in 90 days with an engagement process for a racial equity plan, with Javiera Caballero voting Nay in favor of pausing adoption.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt the conceptual master plan now while directing staff to return within 90 days with a community engagement roadmap to build a racial equity plan before design/construction.
side_a_arguments: Construction is 1.5 to 2 years away, leaving ample time to co-create an equity plan covering affordable housing, local hiring, and corridor engagement before asphalt is laid.

Gentrification is already accelerating citywide regardless of the trail; adopting the master plan preserves federal TIGER/transportation momentum while committing Council to anti-displacement measures.
conflicts.side_b_position: Pause approval of the master plan in deference to community and DOST advocates calling for equity planning first.
side_b_arguments: As a former Durham Open Space and Trails (DOST) commissioner and trail advocate, felt compelled to honor residents and DOST members requesting an explicit pause before adoption.
conflicts.resolution: Motion passed 6-1 at 04:31:15.

conflicts.issue: Proposed Sale of City Property at 700 Canal Street and Potential Trail Access
conflicts.summary: DeDreana Freeman pulled and voted against the sale of 700 Canal Street to Copernica Properties LLC after questioning whether the site had been adequately reviewed for trail access by General Services and Parks and Recreation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the sale of 700 Canal Street to Copernica Properties LLC
side_a_arguments: Staff confirmed General Services and Parks and Recreation had reviewed the parcel for potential trail utilization
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose selling the parcel due to trail access and land-disposition concerns
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman raised questions regarding review for trail purposes and cast the sole vote against the sale
conflicts.resolution: Sale of 700 Canal Street passed 6-1.

conflicts.issue: Fayetteville Commercial Rezoning Without a Development Plan (4510 Fayetteville Road)
conflicts.summary: DeDreana Freeman dissented 6-1 on rezoning 4510 Fayetteville Road to Commercial General without a development plan, contrasting neighborhood-impact concerns against the Hall family's loss of residential viability after MLK Parkway construction.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the FLUM amendment and Commercial General rezoning for 4510 Fayetteville Road
side_a_arguments: City road projects (MLK Jr. Parkway and Fayetteville Road improvements) rendered the five-generation family parcel undevelopable for residential use and restricted to right-in/right-out access
A 300-foot preserved forested stream valley buffers nearby Hanson Road homes
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose open-ended Commercial General rezoning without development-plan restrictions or neighborhood impact tracking
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman noted Council lacked adequate tools to measure neighborhood impacts or restrict future uses without a development plan, making it difficult to favor one property owner over surrounding residents
conflicts.resolution: All three motions for 4510 Fayetteville Road passed 6-1.

conflicts.issue: Downstream Stormwater Flooding Concerns on NC 54 Storage Rezoning (Item 21)
conflicts.summary: DeDreana Freeman cast the sole dissent (6-1) on the CG(D) zoning ordinance for NC 54 Storage after questioning whether stormwater detention elongation could worsen downstream flooding near neighboring apartments.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the NC 54 Storage CG(D) rezoning relying on city stormwater detention and inspection standards
side_a_arguments: Public Works staff Robert Joyner explained stormwater impact analysis requires detention back to pre-development flow rates (up to 100-year storm events when downstream flooding exists)
Steve Schewel noted stormwater ponds are inspected annually and the city cannot ban uphill development solely on general proximity, proposing a stormwater tour for new members
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the CG(D) rezoning over downstream flooding risks to nearby apartments
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman expressed concern about observed flooding near the downstream apartments and potential impacts from elongated stormwater discharge
conflicts.resolution: FLUM and consistency motions passed 7-0, and the CG(D) rezoning ordinance passed 6-1.

conflicts.issue: Item 23: Resolution Approving Public Finance Authority Education Revenue Bonds (Excelsior Classical Academy, up to $20M)
conflicts.summary: Following an intense 50-minute policy debate on charter schools, DPS per-pupil funding, and TeamCFA, the bond resolution failed 2-5 with Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman voting Aye and the remaining five members voting Nay.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 2-5)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (2-5)

conflicts.issue: East Durham Park Tire Mulch Removal Funding Source (General Fund Balance vs. Delaying Piney Wood Soccer Field Repairs)
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-2 over whether to pay $20,000 to remove loose tire mulch at East Durham Park by drawing from the General Fund balance or by following staff's recommendation to delay planned half-penny Parks & Trails repairs to the Piney Wood soccer field for one year.
conflicts.side_a_position: Appropriate $20,000 from General Fund balance so East Durham Park is remediated without delaying Piney Wood or pitting neighborhoods against each other
side_a_arguments: Residents urged not pitting East Durham against another neighborhood's park project
Vernetta Alston noted initial reservations about tapping fund balance but voted Yes to support Council majority for the $20,000 appropriation
conflicts.side_b_position: Follow staff recommendation to delay the Piney Wood soccer field repair by one year instead of tapping General Fund balance
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton argued Piney Wood was a playability/rentability issue rather than a safety hazard and would not be denied, only delayed 12 months
Middleton compared the General Fund balance to a household savings account that should not be raided for a $20,000 project to demonstrate fiscal discipline to taxpayers
conflicts.resolution: Motion to fund loose tire mulch removal via a $20,000 General Fund balance appropriation passed 4-2.

conflicts.issue: Sycamore Street and Bush Drive Permanent Street Closings
conflicts.summary: DeDreana Freeman dissented 5-1 on two permanent street-closing orders (Item 44 Sycamore Street and Item 52 Bush Drive), questioning the high volume of public right-of-way closures coming before Council.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve permanent street-closing orders for unbuilt paper rights-of-way consistent with staff recommendations and prior zoning commitments
side_a_arguments: Both rights-of-way were unbuilt and unmaintained by the city
Staff confirmed Bush Drive closure was required by prior zoning case Z170014 and Sycamore Street was surrounded by TROSA parcels with no agency objections
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose permanent right-of-way closures amid high volume of street closings
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman questioned the unusually large number of street closings appearing on the agenda and voted against closing Sycamore Street and Bush Drive
conflicts.resolution: Both street-closing orders passed 5-1.

conflicts.issue: Piecemeal Rezonings Without Development Plans (Items 22 and 23)
conflicts.summary: DeDreana Freeman cast 5-1 dissents on the Lumley Road zoning ordinance and the Crutchfield Street consistency statement to protest approving speculative rezonings without binding development plans or comprehensive-plan alignment.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the Lumley Road and Crutchfield Street Office/OI rezonings
side_a_arguments: Both sites matched or transitioned cleanly with surrounding OI/industrial zoning
Charlie Reece noted Dan Jewell's UDO analysis confirmed Crutchfield Street setbacks and parking constrained building scale to ~33,000 sq ft even without a development plan
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose piecemeal rezonings lacking development plans or comprehensive-plan updates
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman argued approving rezonings without a developer or development plan represents a harmful piecemeal approach that undermines neighborhood planning
conflicts.resolution: Lumley Road passed 5-1; Crutchfield Street consistency passed 5-1 (with FLUM and zoning passing 6-0).

conflicts.issue: 3404 Page Road Townhome Rezoning and Affordable Housing Proffer (Item 25)
conflicts.summary: DeDreana Freeman voted 5-1 against annexing and rezoning 3404 Page Road for 190 market-rate townhomes, calling the developer's $35,000 affordable housing contribution insufficient when zero units were affordable at 60% AMI.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the 3404 Page Road annexation, FLUM change from Industrial, and PDR 5.78 rezoning with proffered $35,000 housing and $500/student school contributions
side_a_arguments: Planning staff noted surrounding Page Road parcels were already residential and not prime industrial land
Developer proffered landscape buffers, turn lanes, $500 per added DPS student, and $35,000 to the affordable housing fund above legal requirements
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the rezoning over inadequate affordable housing proffers and Page Road traffic
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman noted none of the ~$250,000 townhomes would be affordable at 60% AMI or below and called the $35,000 proffer an insult compared with prior $25,000-per-100-unit benchmarks, while also raising Page Road congestion concerns
conflicts.resolution: All four motions for 3404 Page Road passed 5-1.

conflicts.issue: Immediate Adoption vs. Two-Week Delay on Small Wireless Facilities (5G) Ordinance (Item 13)
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-3 on adopting the small wireless facilities code and fee ordinance immediately versus delaying two weeks after AT&T requested additional time to review House Bill 310 compliance with staff.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt the ordinance immediately and adjust later if needed
side_a_arguments: Public Works staff had already built the permit workflow and were actively receiving 5G small-cell applications without codified local authority
Mark-Anthony Middleton argued the item was vetted at work session, other utilities did not object, and Council should not pause for private offline negotiations
conflicts.side_b_position: Delay action two weeks for stakeholder feedback or oppose HB 310 restrictions
side_b_arguments: Steve Schewel voted No to grant AT&T two weeks of grace so utilities could review the published text
DeDreana Freeman questioned any harm from a two-week delay and raised concerns over HB 310 stripping municipal fee authority over public rights-of-way
conflicts.resolution: Ordinance passed 4-3, with City Manager Tom Bonfield and staff committing to meet with AT&T and bring back any needed amendments.

conflicts.issue: Adopt Ordinance Annexing 1001 Olive Branch Road
conflicts.summary: Following debate over RTP-adjacent urban node planning, voluntary affordable housing and school proffers, and sustainability standards, the annexation ordinance failed 3-4. Staff confirmed the companion rezoning did not need to proceed.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 3-4)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (3-4)

conflicts.issue: Item 23: Ordinance Annexing Carrington Woods (833 Clayton Road) and Utility Extension Agreement

Per the City Attorney, the failure of annexation rendered the consistency and RS-10 rezoning motions moot.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 3-4)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (3-4)

conflicts.issue: Rolling Dale Rezoning Ethics Question and Tree Buffer Continuance
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether Planning Commissioner Neel Ghosh representing the Rolling Dale developer after previously participating at the Planning Commission posed a conflict of interest or public perception concern, and how to balance fairness to the attorney with ethics clarity.
conflicts.side_a_position: Continue the public hearing to August 2018 so the City Attorney can review the Code of Ethics facts and the developer can work with neighbors on tree preservation
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece stated that while he did not believe Mr. Ghosh had improper intent, public perception suffers when a Planning Commissioner later represents an applicant before Council
DeDreana Freeman suggested continuing the item and Steve Schewel proposed keeping the public hearing open until August so clear ethics guidance could be obtained
conflicts.side_b_position: Ensure fairness to Mr. Ghosh by clarifying whether any rule actually barred his appearance rather than leaving innuendo
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton pressed the City Attorney for a definitive statement on whether anything was improper and noted uncertainty over whether existing rules even covered the situation
conflicts.resolution: Without objection, Mayor Schewel kept the public hearing open and continued Item 45 to August 2018 for City Attorney ethics review and further developer-neighborhood talks.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Nov 18, 2019 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: With Council Member Vernetta Alston granted an excused absence (6-0), the Durham City Council on November 18, 2019 approved 6-0 the consent agenda (excluding Item 33) and heard Police Chief Cerelyn Davis's Third Quarter Crime Report (Item 19), where Latinx advocates pressed for lifting U-visa time restrictions and Mayor Schewel committed to action within two weeks. Council voted unanimously 6-0 to designate both Mutual Plaza (Item 20) and the W.C. and Mary Hinton Lyon House (Item 21) as local historic landmarks, and voted 6-0 to approve the Bethpage Office FLUM amendment and rezoning (Item 22) despite Council Member Charlie Reece's reluctance regarding the lack of a development plan. Council also approved 6-0 UDO text amendments for FEMA flood map updates (Item 23) and Omnibus 13 (Item 24), rezoned 1107 Chalk Level Road for 97 townhomes 6-0 (Item 25) while expressing disappointment that neighborhood negotiations removed an affordable housing density bonus, held the FY 2020-2025 Consolidated Plan needs hearing (Item 26), continued the Urban Avenue street closing (Item 27) to December 16, and approved Mayor's Hispanic/Latino Committee appointments 6-0 (Item 33).

agenda_items.title: Neighbor Spotlight, History Moment, Reduce Violence Proclamation, and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Javiera Caballero presented the October Neighbor Spotlight to Anne Drennan for the HELP medical equipment loan program, public historian Eddie Davis delivered a History Moment honoring educator Dr. John Harding Lucas Sr., and Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton read a Reduce Violence Everywhere proclamation accepted by Wanda Boone of Together for Resilient Youth. During announcements, Middleton urged city attention to historic Geer Cemetery upkeep, and City Manager Bonfield highlighted Durham staff panels and awards at the National League of Cities conference.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absences and Consent Agenda (Items 1-18, Pulling Item 33)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 6-0 to grant excused absences to Vernetta Alston for November 18 and to Mayor Schewel for the December 5 work session. After resident Victoria Peterson pulled Item 33 (Mayor's Hispanic/Latino Committee appointments), council approved Consent Agenda Items 1-18 by a 6-0 vote, including the FY 2020-21 budget schedule, CDBG/HOME/HOPWA consolidated plan consultant, Laurel Oaks and Ross Road housing rehabilitations, Veranda at Whitted School ILA, DCLT loan amendment, Durham County Transit Plan grant, Jordan Lake water storage, Cedar Grove shared economic prosperity contract, and a Police Mobile Command Center.

agenda_items.title: 2019 Third Quarter Crime Report and Public Comment on U-Visas and Gun Violence
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Cerelyn Davis reported 32 homicides in the first nine months of 2019 (up from 24 in 2018), a 17% increase in shootings, an 18% decline in sexual assaults, three-year lows in robberies and burglaries, a 5.92-minute average priority-one response time, 97% sworn staffing, and 157 U-visa requests processed YTD (57% approved in Q3). Public speakers voiced conflicting concerns over firearm seizures and stops, funding police hiring and ShotSpotter, and disappointment that DPD had not lifted U-visa time restrictions after six months; Mayor Schewel committed to working with the City Manager and Chief to lift the U-visa limitations within two weeks.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Mutual Plaza Local Historic Landmark Designation (411 W. Chapel Hill St.)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Carla Rosenberg presented the Mutual Plaza landmark request for 1.65 acres covering New Lots 1 and 2 (leaving vacant New Lot 3 undesignated), noting 6-0 Historic Preservation Commission and SHPO support and an estimated $137,000 annual 50% property tax deferral. Council members praised the building's civil rights and Black economic legacy, noted the importance of applying landmark status judiciously, and voted 6-0 to adopt the designation ordinance.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: W.C. and Mary Hinton Lyon House Local Historic Landmark Designation (2423 W. Club Blvd.)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Carla Rosenberg presented the landmark request for the 0.54-acre Prairie/Maya-style W.C. and Mary Hinton Lyon House, submitted by Cynthia de Miranda. Council Member Middleton questioned how council evaluates residential landmarks relative to iconic sites like Mutual Plaza, and de Miranda explained only two examples of the style remain in Durham and the house anchors Club Boulevard's development history. Council voted 6-0 to approve the landmark designation.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Bethpage Office FLUM Amendment and Zoning Map Change (A1800009 / Z1800033)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Emily Struthers presented Tri-Properties' request (represented by Nil Ghosh) to change 23.66 acres at 5621 Chin Page and 3824 Page Road from Industrial Light to Office and Institutional without a development plan, moving the Future Land Use Map from industrial to office/low-medium density residential. While Council Member Charlie Reece expressed strong reservations about approving a rezoning without a development plan, he voted yes alongside colleagues because neighboring Creekside HOA supported removing industrial entitlements. All three required motions passed 6-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 6-0 (FLUM Resolution, Consistency Statement, Zoning Ordinance)

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: UDO Text Amendment TC1900003 (FEMA FIRM Flood Insurance Rate Map Updates)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Michael Stock presented technical UDO revisions adopting updated FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Map panels ahead of a December 6, 2019 deadline to maintain National Flood Insurance Program eligibility, already approved by the Board of County Commissioners on October 28 and Planning Commission 12-0. Resident Helen Plass urged stronger urban forest and stormwater protections around flood zones; council approved the consistency statement and text amendment 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: UDO Text Amendment TC1900001 (Omnibus 13)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Michael Stock presented Omnibus 13 technical and minor policy UDO updates, including EAR, domestic chickens, solar access, excluding ADUs from density calculations, Planning Director authority to suspend UDO rules during declared emergencies, and requiring sidewalks on both sides of suburban-tier streets. Residents Helen Plass and Mimi Kessler objected to electronic notice, excluding ADUs from density, and staff emergency suspension powers, while staff clarified emergency suspension requires a formal mayoral or BOCC state-of-emergency declaration and council praised the new suburban sidewalk mandate. Both motions passed 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Zoning Map Change — 1107 Chalk Level Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jamie Sunyak presented Eagle Point Properties' request (represented by Mike Tarrant of Stewart Inc.) to rezone 12.17 acres from RS-10 to RS-M for up to 97 for-sale townhomes (with 80% capped at 1,500 sq. ft.), a bus pull-out/shelter, and sidewalk gap construction, reduced from 192 apartments after neighborhood meetings. Mayor Pro Tem Johnson and Mayor Schewel supported the project 6-0 while lamenting that neighborhood negotiations had eliminated Durham's first proposed use of the affordable housing density bonus.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: FY 2020-2025 Consolidated Plan Needs Public Hearing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Wilma Conyers of Community Development outlined the HUD consolidated plan timeline and projected FY 2021 entitlement allocations ($1.9M CDBG, $1M HOME, $160k ESG, $429k HOPWA). Resident Victoria Peterson urged coordinating federal funds with the $95 million affordable housing bond to train and hire local workers; no council vote was required.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Urban Avenue Street Closing and Development Agreement (949 Washington St.)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Patrick Young requested continuing the Urban Avenue street closing and Brame Specialty building development agreement due to late applicant easement changes. Mayor Schewel opened the hearing and continued it to December 16, 2019 without objection.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item 33: Mayor's Hispanic/Latino Committee Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Victoria Peterson challenged the committee's racial diversity and questioned whether leadership appointees were U.S. citizens. Mayor Schewel affirmed that Durham welcomes all residents on boards and commissions regardless of documentation status, Council Member Freeman noted a committee of Black and Hispanic residents advanced racial equity, and council approved the appointments 6-0.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Nov 18, 2019 (with closed captions)
meetings.executive_summary: With Council Member Vernetta Alston granted an excused absence (6-0), the Durham City Council on November 18, 2019 approved 6-0 the consent agenda (excluding Item 33) and heard Police Chief Cerelyn Davis's Third Quarter Crime Report (Item 19), where Latinx advocates pressed for lifting U-visa time restrictions and Mayor Schewel committed to action within two weeks. Council voted unanimously 6-0 to designate both Mutual Plaza (Item 20) and the W.C. and Mary Hinton Lyon House (Item 21) as local historic landmarks, and voted 6-0 to approve the Bethpage Office FLUM amendment and rezoning (Item 22) despite Council Member Charlie Reece's reluctance regarding the lack of a development plan. Council also approved 6-0 UDO text amendments for FEMA flood map updates (Item 23) and Omnibus 13 (Item 24), rezoned 1107 Chalk Level Road for 97 townhomes 6-0 (Item 25) while expressing disappointment that neighborhood negotiations removed an affordable housing density bonus, held the FY 2020-2025 Consolidated Plan needs hearing (Item 26), continued the Urban Avenue street closing (Item 27) to December 16, and approved Mayor's Hispanic/Latino Committee appointments 6-0 (Item 33).

agenda_items.title: Neighbor Spotlight, History Moment, Reduce Violence Proclamation, and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Javiera Caballero presented the October Neighbor Spotlight to Anne Drennan for the HELP medical equipment loan program, public historian Eddie Davis delivered a History Moment honoring educator Dr. John Harding Lucas Sr., and Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton read a Reduce Violence Everywhere proclamation accepted by Wanda Boone of Together for Resilient Youth. During announcements, Middleton urged city attention to historic Geer Cemetery upkeep, and City Manager Bonfield highlighted Durham staff panels and awards at the National League of Cities conference.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absences and Consent Agenda (Items 1-18, Pulling Item 33)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 6-0 to grant excused absences to Vernetta Alston for November 18 and to Mayor Schewel for the December 5 work session. After resident Victoria Peterson pulled Item 33 (Mayor's Hispanic/Latino Committee appointments), council approved Consent Agenda Items 1-18 by a 6-0 vote, including the FY 2020-21 budget schedule, CDBG/HOME/HOPWA consolidated plan consultant, Laurel Oaks and Ross Road housing rehabilitations, Veranda at Whitted School ILA, DCLT loan amendment, Durham County Transit Plan grant, Jordan Lake water storage, Cedar Grove shared economic prosperity contract, and a Police Mobile Command Center.

agenda_items.title: 2019 Third Quarter Crime Report and Public Comment on U-Visas and Gun Violence
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Cerelyn Davis reported 32 homicides in the first nine months of 2019 (up from 24 in 2018), a 17% increase in shootings, an 18% decline in sexual assaults, three-year lows in robberies and burglaries, a 5.92-minute average priority-one response time, 97% sworn staffing, and 157 U-visa requests processed YTD (57% approved in Q3). Public speakers voiced conflicting concerns over firearm seizures and stops, funding police hiring and ShotSpotter, and disappointment that DPD had not lifted U-visa time restrictions after six months; Mayor Schewel committed to working with the City Manager and Chief to lift the U-visa limitations within two weeks.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Mutual Plaza Local Historic Landmark Designation (411 W. Chapel Hill St.)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Carla Rosenberg presented the Mutual Plaza landmark request for 1.65 acres covering New Lots 1 and 2 (leaving vacant New Lot 3 undesignated), noting 6-0 Historic Preservation Commission and SHPO support and an estimated $137,000 annual 50% property tax deferral. Council members praised the building's civil rights and Black economic legacy, noted the importance of applying landmark status judiciously, and voted 6-0 to adopt the designation ordinance.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: W.C. and Mary Hinton Lyon House Local Historic Landmark Designation (2423 W. Club Blvd.)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Carla Rosenberg presented the landmark request for the 0.54-acre Prairie/Maya-style W.C. and Mary Hinton Lyon House, submitted by Cynthia de Miranda. Council Member Middleton questioned how council evaluates residential landmarks relative to iconic sites like Mutual Plaza, and de Miranda explained only two examples of the style remain in Durham and the house anchors Club Boulevard's development history. Council voted 6-0 to approve the landmark designation.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Bethpage Office FLUM Amendment and Zoning Map Change (A1800009 / Z1800033)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Emily Struthers presented Tri-Properties' request (represented by Nil Ghosh) to change 23.66 acres at 5621 Chin Page and 3824 Page Road from Industrial Light to Office and Institutional without a development plan, moving the Future Land Use Map from industrial to office/low-medium density residential. While Council Member Charlie Reece expressed strong reservations about approving a rezoning without a development plan, he voted yes alongside colleagues because neighboring Creekside HOA supported removing industrial entitlements. All three required motions passed 6-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 6-0 (FLUM Resolution, Consistency Statement, Zoning Ordinance)

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: UDO Text Amendment TC1900003 (FEMA FIRM Flood Insurance Rate Map Updates)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Michael Stock presented technical UDO revisions adopting updated FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Map panels ahead of a December 6, 2019 deadline to maintain National Flood Insurance Program eligibility, already approved by the Board of County Commissioners on October 28 and Planning Commission 12-0. Resident Helen Plass urged stronger urban forest and stormwater protections around flood zones; council approved the consistency statement and text amendment 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: UDO Text Amendment TC1900001 (Omnibus 13)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Michael Stock presented Omnibus 13 technical and minor policy UDO updates, including EAR, domestic chickens, solar access, excluding ADUs from density calculations, Planning Director authority to suspend UDO rules during declared emergencies, and requiring sidewalks on both sides of suburban-tier streets. Residents Helen Plass and Mimi Kessler objected to electronic notice, excluding ADUs from density, and staff emergency suspension powers, while staff clarified emergency suspension requires a formal mayoral or BOCC state-of-emergency declaration and council praised the new suburban sidewalk mandate. Both motions passed 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Zoning Map Change — 1107 Chalk Level Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jamie Sunyak presented Eagle Point Properties' request (represented by Mike Tarrant of Stewart Inc.) to rezone 12.17 acres from RS-10 to RS-M for up to 97 for-sale townhomes (with 80% capped at 1,500 sq. ft.), a bus pull-out/shelter, and sidewalk gap construction, reduced from 192 apartments after neighborhood meetings. Mayor Pro Tem Johnson and Mayor Schewel supported the project 6-0 while lamenting that neighborhood negotiations had eliminated Durham's first proposed use of the affordable housing density bonus.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: FY 2020-2025 Consolidated Plan Needs Public Hearing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Wilma Conyers of Community Development outlined the HUD consolidated plan timeline and projected FY 2021 entitlement allocations ($1.9M CDBG, $1M HOME, $160k ESG, $429k HOPWA). Resident Victoria Peterson urged coordinating federal funds with the $95 million affordable housing bond to train and hire local workers; no council vote was required.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Urban Avenue Street Closing and Development Agreement (949 Washington St.)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Patrick Young requested continuing the Urban Avenue street closing and Brame Specialty building development agreement due to late applicant easement changes. Mayor Schewel opened the hearing and continued it to December 16, 2019 without objection.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item 33: Mayor's Hispanic/Latino Committee Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Victoria Peterson challenged the committee's racial diversity and questioned whether leadership appointees were U.S. citizens. Mayor Schewel affirmed that Durham welcomes all residents on boards and commissions regardless of documentation status, Council Member Freeman noted a committee of Black and Hispanic residents advanced racial equity, and council approved the appointments 6-0.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Nov 4, 2019 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: With Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton granted an excused absence due to a family health emergency (6-0), the Durham City Council on November 4, 2019 approved excused absences for Middleton and DeDreana Freeman for the November 21 work session (6-0), passed the consent agenda (excluding pulled Items 3 and 21) by a 6-0 vote, and unanimously voted 6-0 across three motions to rezone 12 GoTriangle parcels at 4809 Farrington Road from Light Industrial back to Residential Suburban Multifamily following cancellation of the Durham-Orange Light Rail project. Council held Item 3 (Mayor's Hispanic/Latino Committee appointments) until the November 7 work session without a vote. The majority of the meeting centered on Item 21, the disposition and redevelopment of the former police headquarters at 505 West Chapel Hill Street, where community speakers debated Akridge and New South Ventures' 33% Black ownership stake and higher purchase price against The Fallon Company and WinnCompanies' staff-recommended proposal featuring upfront payment, 4% LIHTC scattered-site affordable housing, and larger commercial office space; council ultimately voted unanimously 6-0 to authorize the City Manager to negotiate a development agreement with The Fallon Company.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absences, Duke Energy Storm Resiliency Grant, History Moment, and Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council granted Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton an excused absence (6-0) due to a family health emergency, accepted a Duke Energy Storm Resiliency Grant for Fire Department swift-water rescue equipment, and heard a History Moment by Eddie Davis honoring Governor William B. Umstead with remarks from his daughter Merle Umstead Ritchie. Council also approved 6-0 excused absences for Council Members Freeman and Middleton for the November 21 work session, heard election reminders ahead of the November 5 municipal election and $95 million housing bond vote, and heard Freeman urge collaboration on youth violence prevention.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Items 3 and 21)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read the consent agenda, with Council Member Freeman pulling Item 3 (Mayor's Hispanic/Latino Committee appointments) and Item 21 (505 West Chapel Hill Street redevelopment) pulled for full discussion. The remaining consent items—including the Triangle Bikeway Implementation Study ILA with Raleigh, water/sewer rehabilitation contracts, condemnation actions, Youth Work Internship Program ILA, National Sexual Assault Kit Initiative grant, Carver Street Extension inspection amendment, and fiber optic network electronics—passed 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Consolidated FLUM Amendment and Zoning Map Change — 4809 Farrington Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jamie Sunyak presented a city-initiated proposal to amend the Future Land Use Map from industrial to low-medium density residential and rezone 12 GoTriangle parcels totaling 23.418 acres on Farrington Road from Light Industrial (previously designated for a light rail operations facility) to RS-M after GoTriangle discontinued the light rail project, noting 12-0 Planning Commission approval. Neighboring residents Ruth Ann McKinney and Philip Post spoke in support of preserving the I-40 tree buffer and watershed protections; council unanimously approved all three required motions 6-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 6-0 (FLUM Resolution, Consistency Statement, Zoning Ordinance)

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item 3: Mayor's Hispanic/Latino Committee Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Freeman noted that absent Council Member Middleton had indicated a vote tally mix-up and wished to review the appointments before voting. Without objection, Mayor Schewel held Item 3 until the Thursday work session.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Held until Thursday work session (No formal vote)

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item 21: Future Disposition and Redevelopment of 505 West Chapel Hill Street
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Project Manager Stacy Poston presented General Services' recommendation to negotiate a development agreement with The Fallon Company (partnered with WinnCompanies, James Rogers, and Dr. Henry McCoy) over finalist Akridge (partnered with New South Ventures). Akridge representatives (Matt Klein, Ken Spaulding, Carl Webb, and Zena Howard) and supporters stressed their $2 million higher offer, single-phase conventional financing, and 33% local Black equity ownership through NSV Development, while Fallon/Winn speakers (Sherrod Banks, Joe Fallon, Gilbert Winn, Shawnie Wilcox, and former Mayor Bill Bell) and staff highlighted upfront cash payment (95% at execution), 4% LIHTC scattered-site affordable housing in perpetuity, and major downtown office capacity. While expressing regret over Fallon's unspecified minority equity percentage and commending Akridge's local equity partnership, all six present council members praised staff's thorough evaluation and voted 6-0 to select The Fallon Company.

Neighboring residents Ruth Ann McKinney and Philip Post spoke in support of preserving the I-40 tree buffer and watershed protections; council unanimously approved all three required motions 6-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 6-0 (FLUM Resolution, Consistency Statement, Zoning Ordinance)

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item 3: Mayor's Hispanic/Latino Committee Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Freeman noted that absent Council Member Middleton had indicated a vote tally mix-up and wished to review the appointments before voting. Without objection, Mayor Schewel held Item 3 until the Thursday work session.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Held until Thursday work session (No formal vote)

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item 21: Future Disposition and Redevelopment of 505 West Chapel Hill Street
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Project Manager Stacy Poston presented General Services' recommendation to negotiate a development agreement with The Fallon Company (partnered with WinnCompanies, James Rogers, and Dr. Henry McCoy) over finalist Akridge (partnered with New South Ventures). Akridge representatives (Matt Klein, Ken Spaulding, Carl Webb, and Zena Howard) and supporters stressed their $2 million higher offer, single-phase conventional financing, and 33% local Black equity ownership through NSV Development, while Fallon/Winn speakers (Sherrod Banks, Joe Fallon, Gilbert Winn, Shawnie Wilcox, and former Mayor Bill Bell) and staff highlighted upfront cash payment (95% at execution), 4% LIHTC scattered-site affordable housing in perpetuity, and major downtown office capacity. While expressing regret over Fallon's unspecified minority equity percentage and commending Akridge's local equity partnership, all six present council members praised staff's thorough evaluation and voted 6-0 to select The Fallon Company.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Oct 21, 2019 (with closed captions)
meetings.executive_summary: At its October 21, 2019 regular meeting presided over by Mayor Steve Schewel with all seven members present, the Durham City Council proclaimed Sister Cities of Durham Week, honored Durham firefighters who built a treehouse through Jamie's Dream Team, inducted the 2019-2020 Durham Youth Commission, recognized Breast Cancer Awareness and National Arts and Humanities Month, and unanimously approved 7-0 the consent agenda. Council voted 7-0 across three motions to approve the High-Fox consolidated annexation and utility extension agreements (Item 22), and voted 7-0 to approve a partial repeal of historic landmark designation for a surface parking parcel at the Brody Duke Warehouse (Item 23), with Mayor Schewel asking the Legislative Committee to review state law capping historic tax-break clawbacks at three years. Council also voted 7-0 to adopt UDO text amendment TC1800005 strengthening tree preservation and landscaping standards (Item 24) while securing staff commitments for follow-up amendments on street trees and commercial preservation, and closed by hearing unscheduled testimony from two Durham Parks and Recreation employees regarding grievance policies, hostile workplace allegations, and camp staffing ratios.

agenda_items.title: Sister Cities Proclamation, Fire Department Recognition, Durham Youth Commission Induction, and Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council proclaimed Sister Cities of Durham Week, recognized Durham Fire Department personnel who partnered with Jamie's Dream Team to build a treehouse for a local child, inducted 14 members of the 2019-2020 Durham Youth Commission featuring spoken-word remarks by Leslie Gonzalez on gentrification, and heard Breast Cancer Awareness and National Arts and Humanities Month presentations from Durham Arts Council Executive Director Sherry DeVries. Council also reminded residents of early voting through November 1 ahead of the November 5 municipal election.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1, 2, and 4-19)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read the consent agenda covering board/commission appointments (Items 2, 4), FY 2018-19 budget carryover ordinances (Item 5), a HOME loan amendment for Willard Street / Cook Road townhomes (Item 6), lift station, dam inspection, wastewater demolition, and water roof contracts (Items 7-10), Chatham County fire/rescue ILA and Duke Energy storm resiliency grant (Items 12-13), Valley Springs Park construction (Item 14), and Carpenter Fletcher and Cornwallis bike/pedestrian design amendments (Items 17, 19). Council approved the consent agenda 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Consolidated Annexation — High-Fox (1106 and 1107 High-Fox Drive)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Emily Struthers presented a voluntary annexation and utility extension request by Sean Gorman for 1.878 acres at 1106 and 1107 High-Fox Drive with exact-translation Rural Residential and Falls/Jordan Watershed Overlay District B zoning effective December 31, 2019. Gorman noted he was present for questions, no opponents spoke, and council approved the annexation/UEA ordinance, consistency statement, and zoning ordinance 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Brody Duke Warehouse Partial Repeal of Landmark Designation (LD1900001, 311 Liggett St.)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Carla Rosenberg presented a request by Measurement Inc. / Greystar (represented by George Stanziale and Brian Sherrick) to repeal historic landmark status from a subdivided 1.46-acre surface parking lot while preserving a 115-foot viewshed around the Brody Duke Warehouse, noting 6-0 Historic Preservation Commission and SHPO support and a statutory three-year back-tax recovery (~$27,000) under NCGS 105-278. Council members questioned green space and tree replacement in the Innovation District, Mayor Schewel asked the Legislative Committee to examine the state's three-year tax clawback cap, and council approved the partial repeal 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: UDO Text Amendment TC1800005 (Tree Coverage and Landscaping Revisions)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Scott Whiteman presented TC1800005 to expand natural project boundary buffers, increase mass-grading buffers in the suburban tier, require preservation of existing trees before replacement planting, raise urban-tier tree coverage, and require one additional lot tree at construction, noting a 10-1 Planning Commission recommendation and a planned street-tree pilot with TreesDurham. Council members sought and received staff confirmation that commercial tree preservation and right-of-way street trees would return in a follow-up text amendment by summer 2020, discussed solar access and mass grading, and approved both the consistency statement and ordinance amendment 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Parks and Recreation Employee Comments on Workplace Conditions and Grievance Policies
agenda_items.discussion_summary: By special exception of Mayor Schewel, Durham Parks and Recreation recreation specialist Kelly McLean and former specialist Chandler Musson testified about hostile management, retaliation, missing written policies, unsafe 1:15 school-age camp staffing ratios, lack of breaks, and an unlocked medication desk, requesting Human Relations and Workers Rights Commission review. Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson confirmed the City Manager launched an ongoing HR/City Manager's Office investigation upon receiving the union's September 25 request, and Schewel thanked the speakers before adjourning at 8:33 p.m.

votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the annexation ordinance and utility extension agreements for 1.878 acres at 1106 and 1107 High-Fox Drive.

votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the exact-translation zoning ordinance for High-Fox.

votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Council repealed landmark status from the subdivided 1.46-acre parking parcel at 311 Liggett Street while preserving the warehouse structure and its 115-foot viewshed.

votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the consistency statement for the tree coverage and landscaping UDO revisions.
