meetings.title: Durham City Council June 17, 2019
meetings.executive_summary: Convening on June 17, 2019 with all seven members present, the Durham City Council honored Jack Price, Ideal Ortiz, and LGBTQ Pride Month pioneers before voting 7-0 to hire Kimberly Martin Rehberg as City Attorney at a $195,000 salary and approving the Consent Agenda 7-0 (excluding pulled Items 9, 13, 20, and 23). Following sharp disagreement over Police Chief C.J. Davis's denied request for 18 sworn officers, Council adopted the $476 million FY 2019-20 budget and FY 2020-25 Capital Improvement Plan (including $15.46/hour living wage for part-time workers, Welcome Home, eviction diversion, and an Office of Equity and Inclusion) by a 6-1 split vote—with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and Mark-Anthony Middleton voting No after Charlie Reece declined Freeman's friendly amendment for nine officers. On Item 27, Council voted 6-1 on both the bond order and referendum resolution to place a $95 million Affordable Housing General Obligation Bond on the November 5, 2019 ballot, with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and DeDreana Freeman voting No. Council concluded by passing pulled Item 9 (Resolution Against White Supremacy, Anti-Semitism, and Islamophobia), Item 13 (HUD lead-based paint grant), Item 20 (Eckerd WIOA youth services), and Item 23 (police psychological testing) unanimously 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Tribute to Jack Price, Neighbor Spotlight, Pride Month, and Hiring of City Attorney Kim Rehberg
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel mourned former council member and affordable housing developer Jack Price, presented the Neighbor Spotlight to Ideal Ortiz, and recognized LGBTQ Pride pioneers Mandy Carter and local advocates. Schewel announced that after a 360-degree review, Council voted 7-0 in closed session to hire Interim City Attorney Kimberly Martin Rehberg at $195,000, then held a public 7-0 vote and swore her in.

agenda_items.title: Manager's Priority Items and Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Items 9, 13, 20, and 23)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield presented minor attachment and title updates for Item 9 and Item 11 (Volunteers of America homelessness diversion), which Council accepted 7-0. With Items 9, 13, 20, and 23 pulled for discussion, Council unanimously adopted the remaining Consent Agenda covering appointments, DCLT and Willard Street/Vermillion affordable housing loans, water/wastewater engineering and mutual aid agreements, Public Works Operations Center renovation, Black Wall Street Gardens public art, and WIOA/NCWorks contracts 7-0.

agenda_items.title: FY 2019-20 Budget and FY 2020-25 Capital Improvement Plan Adoption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Bertha Johnson introduced the $476 million FY 2019-20 budget and FY 2020-25 CIP, after which Jackie Wagstaff, Pastor Rachel Green, Victoria Peterson, Gloria Washington, and Rev. Jerome Washington urged Council to restore Chief C.J. Davis's 18 requested police officers or Mayor Schewel's nine-officer compromise. After Charlie Reece moved adoption, DeDreana Freeman offered a friendly amendment to add nine officers, which Reece declined under Council's single-motion rule. Mark-Anthony Middleton praised living-wage raises and eviction diversion but voted No to register high-crime neighborhoods' call for police staffing, while Schewel, Reece, Jillian Johnson, Vernetta Alston, Javiera Caballero, and Freeman backed the budget (6-1), citing $650,000 for part-time living wages, $3 million for lowest-paid full-time employees, and non-policing investments.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — $95 Million Affordable Housing General Obligation Bond Order and November 5 Referendum
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance Director David Boyd presented the $95 million affordable housing G.O. bond order and referendum resolution for the November 5, 2019 ballot, with Mayor Schewel outlining a 1.2-cent average variable tax scenario versus a 1.6-cent fixed rate. Public speakers Brianna Van Belzen, Marie Hill Faison, and former Mayor Wib Gulley backed placing the bond on the ballot while Victoria Peterson demanded written affordability definitions and senior housing details. Vernetta Alston moved adoption, joined in support by Reece, Johnson, Caballero, Schewel, and Middleton, while DeDreana Freeman voted No on both motions (6-1).

agenda_items.title: Resolution Against White Supremacy, Anti-Semitism, and Islamophobia
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers Robert DeAngelo, Amy Rosenthal, Josh Ravitch, Deborah Friedman, and Rann Bar-On debated the resolution—some criticizing its framing of foreign terrorism or urging Council to rescind its April 2018 ban on Israeli police exchanges, and Bar-On supporting it while urging condemnation of all local ethno-nationalisms. Author Mark-Anthony Middleton (joined by partner Charlie Reece) defended the resolution as an ongoing moral statement against bigotry while clarifying his 2018 vote targeted militarized policing rather than a boycott, read the full text into the record, and Council passed it 7-0.

agenda_items.title: 2018 U.S. HUD Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction and Healthy Homes Program Grant Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Victoria Peterson pulled Item 13 to ask whether the over-$3-million HUD lead abatement grant still included local youth job training and which properties were targeted. City Manager Tom Bonfield offered to respond in writing once she provided a working email address, and Council approved the grant ordinance 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Contract Amendment with Eckerd Youth Alternatives Inc. (Eckerd Connects) for WIOA Youth Services
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Victoria Peterson asked how many youth the program serves and whether it reaches public housing developments like McDougald Terrace and Oxford Manor. Office of Economic and Workforce Development staffer James Dickens confirmed the federally funded program serves 150 youth countywide across Durham, and Council approved the contract amendment 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Contract for Pre-Employment Psychological Testing Services (Durham Police Department)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chris Tiffany spoke against placing psychological testing after conditional employment offers, urging deeper background investigations and broader recruiting at NCCU before issuing provisional offers. Council approved executing the pre-employment psychological testing contract 7-0.

votes.item_title: Hire Kimberly Martin Rehberg as City Attorney at $195,000 Annual Salary
votes.discussion_detail: Following a closed-session 360-degree evaluation and unanimous selection, Council voted 7-0 in open session to hire 15-year city litigator and Interim City Attorney Kimberly Martin Rehberg at a $195,000 salary, and the City Clerk administered her oath of office.

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager's Priority Items (Updates to Item 9 and Item 11)
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously accepted the City Manager's minor title/attachment updates to Item 9 and Item 11 by a 7-0 vote.

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda (Items 1-8, 10-12, 14-19, 21-22, 24-25, 35, excluding pulled Items 9, 13, 20, and 23)
votes.discussion_detail: Excluding pulled Items 9, 13, 20, and 23, Council unanimously adopted the Consent Agenda 7-0.

votes.item_title: Adopt FY 2019-20 Annual Budget, FY 2020-25 Capital Improvement Plan, and Related Ordinances
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton clarified on the record that closed-caption graphics briefly obscured his vote display.
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved adoption of the $476 million budget without the Police Chief's requested 18 new sworn officers (declining DeDreana Freeman's friendly amendment to add 9 officers). Council approved the budget 6-1, with Mark-Anthony Middleton voting No to protest the omission of new police positions for high-crime communities despite supporting the budget's wage and housing investments.

votes.item_title: Item 27 — Adopt Bond Order Authorizing Issuance of Not More Than $95 Million in Affordable Housing General Obligation Bonds
votes.discussion_detail: Vernetta Alston moved adoption of the $95 million affordable housing G.O. bond order after public hearing testimony and finance scenarios from David Boyd and Mayor Schewel; the motion passed 6-1 with DeDreana Freeman voting No.

votes.item_title: Item 27 — Adopt Resolution Setting Special Bond Referendum on $95 Million Affordable Housing Bond for November 5, 2019 Ballot
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the companion resolution placing the $95 million affordable housing bond referendum on the November 5, 2019 ballot 6-1, with DeDreana Freeman voting No.

votes.item_title: Item 9 — Adopt Resolution Against White Supremacy, Anti-Semitism, and Islamophobia
votes.discussion_detail: After five public speakers debated the resolution's language and the Council's April 2018 police-exchange resolution, author Mark-Anthony Middleton read the text into the record and Council unanimously adopted the resolution 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 13 — Adopt Grant Project Ordinance for 2018 U.S. HUD Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction and Healthy Homes Program Grant
votes.discussion_detail: Following questions from Victoria Peterson regarding job training and targeted housing sites, Council adopted the HUD lead-hazard grant project ordinance 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 20 — Authorize City Manager to Execute Contract Amendment with Eckerd Youth Alternatives Inc. (Eckerd Connects) for WIOA Youth Services
votes.discussion_detail: After James Dickens confirmed the federal WIOA contract serves 150 youth countywide, Council approved the contract amendment 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 23 — Authorize Execution of Contract for Police Pre-Employment Psychological Testing Services
votes.discussion_detail: Following public comment by Chris Tiffany urging stronger pre-offer background checks, Council unanimously authorized the pre-employment psychological testing contract 7-0.

disagreements.issue: Police Officer Staffing (18 or 9 Sworn Officers) vs. Living Wage and Non-Policing Priorities in FY 2019-20 Budget
disagreements.summary: Council divided over excluding Police Chief C.J. Davis's request for 18 new sworn officers (and declining a 9-officer compromise) in favor of funding living wages for part-time city employees and equity/housing programs without raising property taxes, passing the budget 6-1.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt the $476 million FY 2019-20 budget without adding 18 new sworn police officers, prioritizing a $15.46/hour living wage for part-time staff, low-wage full-time raises, eviction diversion, and housing/equity programs without a property tax hike.
side_a_arguments: With limited revenue tools outside property taxes that burden low-income and older homeowners, funding both 18 new officers and part-time living wages was not feasible without raising taxes.

The $60 million police budget already absorbs 15 grant-funded sworn positions and adds two latent print examiners; resources are urgently needed for living wages ($650,000), Welcome Home ($200,000), eviction diversion, and the new Office of Equity and Inclusion.

Mayor Schewel noted he had supported a 9-officer compromise for shift relief and training, while DeDreana Freeman offered a friendly amendment for 9 officers (declined by Charlie Reece under single-motion rules) before joining the 6-vote majority.
disagreements.side_b_position: Vote No on the budget to protest omitting new patrol officers requested by Chief Davis and residents in high-gun-violence neighborhoods.
side_b_arguments: Over-policing stems from posture and leadership rather than headcount; proactive staffing is what maintains positive safety metrics.

Denying police staffing in high-crime communities like Cornwallis Road, Oxford Manor, and McDougald Terrace reflects a 'pecking order' in progressive politics that ignores vulnerable residents' pleas.
disagreements.resolution: Friendly amendment for 9 officers was declined by mover Charlie Reece; the FY 2019-20 budget and CIP passed 6-1 with Mark-Anthony Middleton voting No.

disagreements.issue: $95 Million Affordable Housing General Obligation Bond Order and Referendum (Item 27)
disagreements.summary: Council voted 6-1 on both the bond order and referendum resolution to place a $95 million Affordable Housing General Obligation Bond on the November 5, 2019 ballot, with DeDreana Freeman casting the sole No vote.
disagreements.side_a_position: Place the $95 million Affordable Housing Bond on the November 2019 ballot to fund thousands of affordable units, DHA redevelopment, eviction diversion, and homelessness prevention.
side_a_arguments: Routine annual operating funds cannot overcome market-driven gentrification and displacement.
The bond leverages Durham's tax base at an estimated 1.2-cent average variable (or 1.6-cent fixed) tax rate to build lasting nonprofit and Durham Housing Authority capacity.
disagreements.side_b_position: Vote No on the $95 million bond order and November referendum resolution.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman recorded No votes on both the bond order and special referendum resolution without delivering floor remarks explaining her dissent (following public comment concerns from Victoria Peterson seeking written affordability definitions and senior housing guarantees).
disagreements.resolution: Both the bond order and referendum resolution passed 6-1, with DeDreana Freeman voting No.

meetings.title: Durham City Council June 3, 2019
meetings.executive_summary: Convening on June 3, 2019 with all seven members present, the Durham City Council recognized Pride Month on the 50th anniversary of the Stonewall riots and celebrated Participatory Budgeting (PB Durham) exceeding 10,000 voters across three ballots allocating $2.4 million. Council voted 7-0 to approve the City Manager's priority request referring Item 13 (Community Empowerment Fund landlord engagement contract) back to administration for minor contract-language revisions, and reviewed the Consent Agenda with Items 8, 9, and 22 pulled. On a contested annexation ordinance for 1001 Olive Branch Road, Council split 3-4 with Steve Schewel, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and Javiera Caballero, Jillian Johnson, DeDreana Freeman, and Charlie Reece voting No over sustainability and planning standards, halting the companion rezoning. At the close of the meeting, Council voted 7-0 to authorize an economic development incentive agreement with Famous Chicken Hut Durham, Inc. to help sustain the historic Fayetteville Street restaurant.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Pride Month Proclamation, and Participatory Budgeting Milestone
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m., Council Member Charlie Reece led the Pledge of Allegiance, and the clerk recorded all seven members present. Council presented a Pride Month proclamation marking the 50th anniversary of the Stonewall riots and celebrated PB Durham surpassing its 10,000-voter goal across $2.4 million in community-selected projects.

agenda_items.title: Referral of Item 13 (Community Empowerment Fund Landlord Engagement) Back to Administration
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager requested referring Item 13—approving dedicated housing funds for the Community Empowerment Fund for landlord engagement—back to administration due to a minor contract language issue, noting it was expected back at Thursday's work session. Council voted 7-0 to approve the referral.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review (Items 1–36 and Item 50; Items 8, 9, 13, and 22 Removed)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read Consent Agenda Items 1–36 and Item 50, noting Items 8 (FY18-19 budget amendment), 9 (Racial Equity Task Force initial report), and 22 ($95 million GO bond referendum) were pulled and Item 13 was referred back. Council also briefly noted letterhead formatting on Item 50 (Durham Economic Justice Resolution), while the final consent vote occurred in an omitted portion of the digest.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (consent vote omitted in digest)

agenda_items.title: Annexation and Rezoning for 1001 Olive Branch Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated annexing and rezoning 1001 Olive Branch Road near Research Triangle Park, weighing Planning Commissioners' comments on urban node creation and voluntary affordable housing and school proffers against comprehensive plan and sustainability shortcomings. The annexation ordinance failed 3-4, after which staff confirmed Council did not need to act on the companion rezoning.

agenda_items.title: Economic Development Incentive Agreement with Famous Chicken Hut Durham, Inc.
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Economic development staff (Chris Dickey) presented an incentive agreement to support Famous Chicken Hut at 1319 Fayetteville Street following the passing of matriarch Peggy Tapp and generational transition to her son and cousin Jeffrey Johnson. Following appreciative remarks from Council and owners, Council voted 7-0 to authorize the City Manager to execute the agreement.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager's Priority Item Referring Item 13 (Community Empowerment Fund Contract) Back to Administration
votes.discussion_detail: Council voted 7-0 to refer Item 13 back to administration to resolve a minor contract language issue before bringing it to the Thursday work session.

votes.item_title: Adopt Ordinance Annexing 1001 Olive Branch Road
votes.notes: Clerk announced Javiera Caballero, Jillian Johnson, DeDreana Freeman, and Charlie Reece voting no.
votes.discussion_detail: Following debate over RTP-adjacent urban node planning, voluntary affordable housing and school proffers, and sustainability standards, the annexation ordinance failed 3-4. Staff confirmed the companion rezoning did not need to proceed.

votes.item_title: Authorize City Manager to Execute Economic Development Incentive Agreement with Famous Chicken Hut Durham, Inc.
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously authorized an economic development incentive agreement to support structural and continuity needs for the 60-year-old Fayetteville Street restaurant.

disagreements.issue: 1001 Olive Branch Road Annexation and Urban Node Rezoning
disagreements.summary: Council divided 3-4 over whether to annex and rezone 1001 Olive Branch Road near Research Triangle Park, weighing existing comprehensive plan alignment and voluntary proffers against sustainability and growth-management expectations.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support annexation and rezoning as consistent with existing precedent and RTP-adjacent growth.
side_a_arguments: Proximity to Research Triangle Park supports creating an urban node in the area.
The applicant's voluntary proffers for affordable housing and Durham Public Schools followed established precedent.
The proposal met current legal and comprehensive plan standards rather than justifying an ad hoc denial.
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny annexation because the project falls short on sustainability and comprehensive plan expectations.
side_b_arguments: Even where current comprehensive plan rules allow it, developers must meet higher sustainability standards.
Approving projects that fail long-term sustainability and generational stewardship principles prevents better development outcomes.
Any urban node in this corridor needs to be planned properly before extending city annexation.
disagreements.resolution: The annexation ordinance failed 3-4, ending consideration of the companion rezoning.

meetings.title: Durham City Council May 20, 2019
meetings.executive_summary: At its May 20, 2019 meeting, the Durham City Council honored former Mayor Wense Grabarek on the anniversary of his 1963 inauguration, proclaimed June 7, 2019 as National Gun Violence Awareness Day with Council Member Vernetta Alston and Moms Demand Action, and reminded residents age 13 and older to vote in Participatory Budgeting. Council pulled Items 14 and 15 from the Consent Agenda, then unanimously passed 7-0 a federal tax-law resolution for Capital Trust Agency Series 2019 revenue bonds, an ordinance aligning stormwater development standards with state law and the city's NPDES permit, and Item 14 adopting FY 2019-20 water and sewer rates. On pulled Item 15 authorizing Local Government Commission (LGC) application and notice resolutions for a $95 million General Obligation bond referendum, Council voted 6-1 to advance the resolutions, with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and DeDreana Freeman voting No due to timing, fixed-income affordability, and housing authority displacement concerns.

agenda_items.title: Honoring Former Mayor Wense Grabarek, Gun Violence Awareness Proclamation, and PB Durham Reminder
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel and guests honored former Mayor Wense Grabarek on the anniversary of his May 20, 1963 inauguration, highlighting his 1963 biracial dialogue and major economic and annexation milestones. Council Member Vernetta Alston read the National Gun Violence Awareness Day proclamation honoring Durham victims, and Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton joined a presentation while residents 13+ were urged to vote in PB Durham.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review (Items 1–28; Items 14 and 15 Pulled)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With no priority items from staff, Mayor Schewel read Consent Agenda Items 1–28 covering board appointments, water and street contracts, DPAC audio upgrades, and affordable housing loans. Items 14 (FY19-20 water and sewer rates) and 15 ($95 million GO bond referendum) were pulled for separate action; the consent vote itself was omitted in digest truncation.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (consent vote omitted in digest)

agenda_items.title: Capital Trust Agency Tax-Exempt Revenue Bond Series 2019 Resolution
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff explained the host-jurisdiction public hearing required under federal tax law for Capital Trust Agency Series 2019 revenue bonds, noting the city carries no repayment obligation or financial impact. No public speakers appeared, and Council voted 7-0 to adopt the resolution.

agenda_items.title: Ordinance Amending Stormwater Performance Standards for Development
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Stormwater staff presented code amendments to align with the city's October 10, 2018 NPDES permit and state session laws that barred local enforcement of Jordan Lake nutrient rules on new development, substituting total suspended solids as a pollutant surrogate while retaining Falls Lake rules. Consultant Tim Savers spoke in support, and Council adopted the ordinance 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Ordinance Adopting Water and Sewer Rates for FY 2019-20

agenda_items.title: $95 Million General Obligation Bond Referendum Resolutions (LGC Application and Notice of Intent)

votes.item_title: Adopt Resolutions for Notice of Intent, LGC Application, and Statements of Fact for $95 Million General Obligation Bond Referendum (Item 15)
votes.notes: Audio ASR rendered 'Council Member Freeman voting no' as 'the item of agreement voting no'.
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the three required procedural resolutions to apply to the Local Government Commission for the $95 million GO bond referendum, with DeDreana Freeman dissenting over timing and displacement concerns.

disagreements.issue: Timing and Displacement Risks of $95 Million General Obligation Bond Referendum (Item 15)
disagreements.summary: Council voted 6-1 to advance procedural Local Government Commission filings for the $95 million General Obligation bond referendum, with DeDreana Freeman urging a one-year delay to protect fixed-income and public-housing residents.
disagreements.side_a_position: Advance the $95 million GO bond LGC filings on the current schedule.
side_a_arguments: Proceeding with notice of intent and LGC application keeps the $95 million bond referendum on track for the current cycle.
The bond package reflects figures outlined in the Mayor's letter to Council.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defer the $95 million bond referendum until the next cycle pending anti-displacement and tax-relief measures.
side_b_arguments: Advancing the bond alongside other cost and rate increases creates financial strain for fixed-income residents without clear relief levers.
An economic development plan should be established before moving forward.
Federal housing authority desegregation pushes are driving displacement of predominantly African-American housing authority residents.
disagreements.resolution: Resolutions passed 6-1, with DeDreana Freeman voting no.

meetings.executive_summary: Meeting on May 6, 2019, the Durham City Council recognized local and state student contest winners, heard a Sesquicentennial history moment on Chief Justice Earl Warren and Brown v. agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 2–33, Excluding Pulled Item 6)

meetings.title: Durham City Council Mar 18, 2019
meetings.executive_summary: Meeting on March 18, 2019 with six members present after Charlie Reece moved and Council unanimously granted Javiera Caballero an excused absence to attend a funeral in Charlotte, the Durham City Council honored Southwest Central Durham volunteer Rena Pennix and passed a 17-item Consent Agenda including utility contracts and Durham Station bus leases. Budget Director Bertha Johnson opened the FY 2019-20 budget and FY 2020-25 CIP public hearing by reporting a 20.76% countywide property value increase from the January 2019 reappraisal, followed by public speakers including Beth Brooke opposing proposed funding for 72 new police officers. Later in the evening, Council voted 6-0 across three motions to annex and rezone 301 Atkins Heights Boulevard despite neighbor objections over extending Marcy Road, voted 6-0 on Item 27 updating the Durham-Raleigh annexation and utility boundary agreement, and voted 6-0 to amend Chapter 62 allowing city acceptance of developer-built public trails.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absence for Javiera Caballero, Neighborhood Spotlight (Rena Pennix), and Meals on Wheels
agenda_items.discussion_summary: On a motion by Charlie Reece, Council unanimously granted Javiera Caballero an excused absence for the meeting while she attended a funeral in Charlotte. Council then presented the March Neighborhood Spotlight to Rena Pennix of Southwest Central Durham for food bank, community garden, and traffic-calming work, and heard an announcement encouraging Meals on Wheels volunteers.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1–17)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With no items pulled, Council unanimously approved Consent Agenda Items 1–17 covering Planning Commission and DPAC oversight reappointments, pipeline and sewer repair contracts, cross-connection electronic filing fees, Megabus and Greyhound leases at Durham Station, and the Lodge Street Regional Stormwater amendment.

agenda_items.title: FY 2019-20 Budget and FY 2020-25 Capital Improvement Plan Public Hearing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Bertha Johnson reported that the January 2019 reappraisal increased city real property assessed values by 20.76% over the current 57.8-cent tax rate. Seventeen speakers signed up; Beth Brooke urged Council to honor its 2018 'Durham Beyond Policing' resolution by rejecting funding for 72 new police officers and investing in education, affordable housing, and participatory budgeting.

agenda_items.title: Annexation and Zoning Map Change for 301 Atkins Heights Boulevard (Epcon Development)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Neighbors objected to extending Marcy Road into the proposed Epcon development due to cut-through traffic, emergency vehicle access, and paving costs, while Transportation staff Bill Judge explained the UDO mandates the street connection and allows traffic-calming review at site plan. Council approved the annexation, consistency statement, and UDO amendment 6-0 across three votes.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Durham-Raleigh Sanitary/Water Service Areas and Annexation Boundary Agreement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Grace Smith presented minor right-of-way alignment updates to the 1999 Durham-Raleigh annexation agreement ahead of Raleigh's April 2 hearing, and speaker Nelson Paul commented on jurisdiction along the line. Council voted 6-0 to authorize the Mayor to execute the agreement.

agenda_items.title: Ordinance Amending Chapter 62 for Acceptance of Developer-Built Public Trails
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works representative Robert Joyner presented code changes allowing private developers to dedicate trail easements, build trails to city standards, and petition Council for public acceptance and maintenance like streets. After clarifying questions from Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson confirming public ownership, Council adopted the ordinance 6-0.

votes.item_title: Grant Excused Absence to Council Member Javiera Caballero
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved to grant Javiera Caballero an excused absence to attend a funeral in Charlotte; the six present members approved unanimously by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Adopt Ordinance Annexing 301 Atkins Heights Boulevard
votes.notes: Mayor initially misread the vote as 4-2 before immediately correcting it to 6-0.
votes.discussion_detail: Council approved annexation of 301 Atkins Heights Boulevard for the Epcon development following public comment on Marcy Road connectivity.

votes.item_title: Adopt Consistency Statement for 301 Atkins Heights Boulevard Zoning Map Change
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously adopted the comprehensive plan consistency statement for 301 Atkins Heights Boulevard.

votes.item_title: Adopt Ordinance Amending the UDO for 301 Atkins Heights Boulevard
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously adopted the UDO zoning map amendment for 301 Atkins Heights Boulevard.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Mar 4, 2019
meetings.executive_summary: Convening on March 4, 2019 with all seven members present, the Durham City Council recognized outgoing City Attorney Patrick Baker alongside former Mayor Bill Bell, welcomed Interim City Attorney Kim Rehberg, issued Disability and Women's History/ERA proclamations, and passed the Consent Agenda 7-0. Police Chief C.J. Davis presented Item 19, the 2018 fourth-quarter and annual crime report, noting a 7% drop in Part 1 index crime, a 13% drop in violent crime, and a 6% drop in property crime. In zoning public hearings, Council denied a 30-day continuance request from an adjacent owner alleging private deed restrictions on Davis Park West and approved both the consistency statement and UDO amendment 7-0. On Item 21 (1020 Hale Street duplex rezoning), Council voted 6-1 on both the consistency statement and UDO amendment, with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and DeDreana Freeman voting No.

agenda_items.title: Girl Scouts Pledge, Proclamations, Tribute to City Attorney Patrick Baker, and Neighborhood Spotlight
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Ten Girl Scout troops led the Pledge of Allegiance, followed by proclamations for disability inclusion and Women's History Month/the Equal Rights Amendment and remarks from Judge Allyson Kay Duncan. Former Mayor Bill Bell joined Mayor Schewel in honoring retiring City Attorney Patrick Baker, Tony Simpson received the Neighborhood Spotlight, and Interim City Attorney Kim Rehberg was introduced.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1–17 and Item 28)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With no priority items or pulls, Council unanimously passed the Consent Agenda 7-0, covering an RDU Airport Authority appointment, timekeeping audit, CDBG/HOME reimbursements, DOLRT plan review amendment, Hoover Road Athletic Park CMAR contract with Skanska USA Building, and a Made in Durham youth pipeline contract.

agenda_items.title: 2018 Fourth Quarter and Annual Crime Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief C.J. Davis delivered an oral 2018 annual crime report (due to Q3 slides appearing on screen), reporting that compared to 2017, Part 1 index crime declined 7%, Part 1 violent crime fell 13%, property crime fell 6%, and firearm involvement in aggravated assaults dropped from 68% to 59%.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — Davis Park West
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Cynthia White, representing adjacent Republic Flats Apartments/Eaton Vance, sought a 30-day continuance claiming lack of notice and private commercial-only deed restrictions, which developer Craig Davis's representative rebutted with October 2018 emails and Boston meeting records. Viewing private deed covenants as outside municipal zoning authority, Council passed both the consistency statement and UDO ordinance 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — 1020 Hale Street Duplex
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Emily Stravitz presented Martin McFarling's request to rezone 1020 Hale Street from RU-5 to RU-5(2) for duplexes, consistent with the Medium Density Residential future land use map. Applicant Marty McFarling cited bank financing barriers for a single-family plus ADU setup, while opponent William Whitmore opposed duplex zoning; Council passed both motions 6-1 with DeDreana Freeman voting No.

votes.item_title: Adopt Consistency Statement for Davis Park West Zoning Map Change
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the consistency statement for Davis Park West after declining an adjacent owner's 30-day continuance request.

votes.item_title: Adopt Ordinance Amending the UDO for Davis Park West
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously adopted the UDO zoning amendment ordinance for Davis Park West.

votes.item_title: Adopt Consistency Statement for 1020 Hale Street Duplex Zoning Map Change (Item 21)
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the consistency statement for the 1020 Hale Street duplex rezoning 6-1, with DeDreana Freeman voting no.

votes.item_title: Adopt Ordinance Amending the UDO for 1020 Hale Street Duplex (Item 21)
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the UDO amendment rezoning 1020 Hale Street to RU-5(2) by a 6-1 vote, with DeDreana Freeman dissenting.

disagreements.issue: 1020 Hale Street Duplex Rezoning (Item 21)
disagreements.summary: Council voted 6-1 to rezone 1020 Hale Street from RU-5 to RU-5(2) for duplexes, with DeDreana Freeman opposing both the consistency statement and UDO amendment following neighbor opposition and Planning Commission questions.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve rezoning 1020 Hale Street to RU-5(2) for duplex development.
side_a_arguments: The rezoning aligns with the Medium Density Residential designation on the future land use map.
Applicant Marty McFarling explained banks would not finance nonconforming construction or treat a single-family home with an ADU equivalently to a duplex.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose rezoning 1020 Hale Street to RU-5(2).
side_b_arguments: Opposed both the consistency statement and UDO amendment after public opposition from William Whitmore regarding rental and neighborhood impacts and Planning Commission discussion of existing single-family/ADU zoning.
disagreements.resolution: Both the consistency statement and UDO amendment passed 6-1, with DeDreana Freeman voting no.

meetings.title: City Council Meeting   Feb 4, 2019 (No Pledge of Allegiance)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presided over the brief February 4, 2019 regular meeting of the Durham City Council, opening with a moment of silent meditation and two ceremonial proclamations. The council declared February 2019 as Together for Resilient Youth (TRY) Prevention Month—highlighting youth substance-use trends and alcohol retailer compliance—and Council Member Charlie Reece presented a proclamation recognizing January 30, 2019 as Fred Korematsu Day of Civil Liberties and the Constitution. During announcements, Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton noted a recent staff presentation on ShotSpotter gunshot detection technology while emphasizing no decision had been made, and Council Member Javiera Caballero announced a February 24 public safety forum focused on the immigrant and Latino community. Following no priority items from staff, the council voted unanimously 7-0 to approve the five-item consent agenda before adjourning at 7:23 p.m.

agenda_items.title: Together for Resilient Youth (TRY) Prevention Month Proclamation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the meeting to order, led a moment of silent meditation, and read a proclamation declaring February 2019 as Together for Resilient Youth (TRY) Prevention Month, citing data from the 2017 Durham County Youth Risk Behavior Survey. Earl Boone accepted the proclamation on behalf of TRY, highlighting reductions in youth substance use outside of marijuana, praising TRY's Good Neighbor Business Network alcohol compliance efforts and CDC recognition, and warning of risks from adolescent marijuana use.

agenda_items.title: Fred Korematsu Day of Civil Liberties and the Constitution Proclamation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Charlie Reece introduced and read a proclamation declaring January 30, 2019 as Fred Korematsu Day of Civil Liberties and the Constitution, reflecting on World War II Japanese American internment under Executive Order 9066 and his own family's immigration history. Dr. Chiyoko Lord of the Japan-America Society of North Carolina accepted the proclamation and emphasized the importance of remembering civil rights struggles.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements (ShotSpotter Briefing, Latino Public Safety Forum) and Staff Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton congratulated colleagues on their LGBTQ Center benefit at Pinhook, recognized Council Member Javiera Caballero's Durham Magazine feature and Black History Month events, and thanked the City Manager for arranging a recent presentation on ShotSpotter technology while noting no decisions had been made. Council Member Charlie Reece recognized former Council Member Jackie Wagstaff in attendance, and Council Member Caballero announced a February 24 public safety forum at Immaculata featuring Police Chief Cerelyn Davis, District Attorney Satana Deberry, and Sheriff Clarence Birkhead to address crimes targeting the immigrant and Latino community. The City Manager, City Attorney Kim Rehberg, and City Clerk reported no priority items.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1, 3, 4, 6, and 7)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read the consent agenda comprising approval of City Council minutes (Item 1), the December 2018 bid report (Item 3), a three-year renewal of the right-of-way maintenance and mowing contract (Item 4), a Building Inspections Land Development Office web portal upgrade (Item 6), and an ESRI software maintenance service agreement (Item 7). No items were pulled by council members or the public, and the council approved the consent agenda unanimously.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Jan 22, 2019
meetings.executive_summary: At the January 22, 2019 regular meeting presided over by Mayor Steve Schewel, the Durham City Council began with ceremonial recognitions and heard from a nonprofit providing free school supplies to Durham Public Schools teachers ahead of a citywide supply drive. Following introductions from new City Attorney Kim Rehberg and no priority items, the council voted unanimously 7-0 to adopt a consent agenda covering the 2019 Long Session Legislative Agenda, bicycle lane striping, waterline and street/bridge infrastructure contracts, a HIDTA grant amendment, an MLK Jr. Commission grant, and the Durham Workers Rights Commission scope and composition. In two public hearings without public speakers, the council unanimously voted 7-0 on both the consistency statement and ordinance for UDO text amendment TC18008 allowing limited text-only development plans, and voted 7-0 to adopt amendments to the Durham Comprehensive Plan's Future Land Use Map and policies.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Ceremonial Proclamation, and Nonprofit School Supply Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the meeting to order and presented a proclamation recognizing a longtime community champion. Representatives from a local nonprofit also spoke about supplying free school materials to teachers across more than 50 Durham Public Schools and partnering with city departments to place donation bins throughout city facilities.

agenda_items.title: Introduction of City Attorney Kim Rehberg and Staff Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Incoming City Attorney Kim Rehberg introduced herself in place of outgoing City Attorney Patrick Baker and reported no priority items. The City Clerk also reported no priority items.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1-7 and 14, including Legislative Agenda, Streets/Water Contracts, and Workers Rights Commission)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read the consent agenda, which included the 2019 Long Session Legislative Agenda (Item 1), a bicycle lane striping agreement TIP C-5605E (Item 2), American Tobacco District waterline replacement Amendment No. 3 (Item 3), a 2018 HIDTA grant ordinance amendment (Item 4), Contract ST-271 for 2018 Petition Streets (Item 5), Contract ST-288B for a city-maintained bridge asset management plan (Item 6), the Durham Workers Rights Commission proposed scope and composition (Item 7), and an NC Martin Luther King Jr. Commission grant (Item 14). Audience members applauded following the council's unanimous approval of the consent slate.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: UDO Text Amendment TC18008 (Text-Only Development Plans)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Michael Stock of the Planning Department presented text amendment TC18008, creating a limited text-only development plan option for zoning map change requests to permit proffers restricting allowed uses while broader revisions are developed. He noted prior review by the Joint City-County Planning Committee, a 12-0 Planning Commission recommendation, and January 14 approval by the Board of County Commissioners. No members of the public spoke during the hearing, a council member thanked planning staff for timely work, and the council approved both the consistency statement and the ordinance amendment 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: 2017 Evaluation and Assessment Report of the Durham Comprehensive Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Laurie Woods of the Planning Department presented proposed Future Land Use Map and policy amendments from the 2017 Comprehensive Plan Evaluation and Assessment Report, including three parcels providing a direct connection between the state park and Valley Springs Park. No members of the public spoke during the hearing; council members asked about engagement strategy and discussed Planning Commission feedback—specifically Commissioner Miller's concern about burdens on Neighborhood Protection Overlays (NPOs) and historic districts after staff removed a mandatory denial recommendation tied to affordability impacts. The council closed the hearing and adopted the resolution amending the Future Land Use Map and policies 7-0.

votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the public hearing with no public speakers, council adopted the required consistency statement (Attachment A) for UDO text amendment TC18008.

votes.item_title: Item 8: Ordinance Amending the UDO (Text Amendment TC18008 — Text-Only Development Plans)
votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted Attachment B amending the Unified Development Ordinance to allow limited text-only development plans for zoning map change requests.

votes.item_title: Item 9: Resolution Amending Future Land Use Map and Policies of the Durham Comprehensive Plan (2017 Evaluation and Assessment Report)
votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: After closing the public hearing with no public speakers and discussing Planning staff engagement and Planning Commission feedback on Neighborhood Protection Overlays and historic districts, council adopted the resolution amending the Future Land Use Map and policies.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Jan 7, 2019
meetings.executive_summary: At its first meeting of 2019 on January 7, the Durham City Council recognized Durham Parks and Recreation staff, a local international youth chess champion, Martin Luther King Jr. Day commemoration events, and January as National Mentoring Month with remarks from the Emily K Center. Council voted 7-0 to refer Agenda Item 9 (unarmed security guard services for city parking facilities) back to the City Manager's office, and City Attorney Patrick Baker read his resignation notice effective March 8, 2019 after 21 years of service to Durham. Council unanimously approved 7-0 the consent agenda (excluding Items 3, 8, and 9) covering transportation planning agreements, hazard mitigation grants, board changes, and travel policy. Following public comment from resident Victoria Peterson on Items 3 and 8 regarding youth programming, community centers, and economic development, the council voted 7-0 to approve both the Bloomberg Mayor's Challenge Grant (Item 3) and Item 8.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Silent Meditation, Pledge of Allegiance, and Roll Call
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the January 7, 2019 meeting to order, wished residents a happy New Year, and led a moment of silent meditation. Council Member Charlie Reece led the Pledge of Allegiance, and the City Clerk called the roll confirming the attendance of council members.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations and Recognitions (DPR, Youth Chess Champion, MLK Events, National Mentoring Month)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel and the council presented proclamations and recognitions, beginning with remarks thanking Durham Parks and Recreation employees, the City Manager, and Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson. The council honored a local youth chess champion competing internationally who discussed empowering girls in chess, announced upcoming Martin Luther King Jr. Day events including the January 21 interfaith prayer breakfast, and proclaimed January 2019 National Mentoring Month with remarks from an Emily K Center representative.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Item: Refer Agenda Item 9 (Parking Facilities Security Guard Services) Back to Administration
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Bonfield requested as a priority item that Agenda Item 9—uniformed unarmed security guard services for the city's parking facilities—be referred back to the administration. Council voted unanimously 7-0 to refer the item back to the City Manager's office.

agenda_items.title: City Attorney Patrick Baker Resignation Announcement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Reporting no priority items, City Attorney Patrick Baker requested personal privilege to read his resignation letter submitted during an earlier 6:00 p.m. closed session, giving notice effective March 8, 2019. Mayor Schewel praised Baker's 21 years of service as both City Manager and City Attorney and wished him well in his new role in Charlotte, and the City Clerk reported no priority items.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Items 3, 8, and 9)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read the consent agenda including minutes (Item 1), Historic Preservation Commission appointment (Item 2), Elected Officials Travel Authorization and Expense Reimbursement Policy (Item 4), Environmental Affairs Board expansion (Item 6), a Phase Two developer agreement and option contract (Item 7), DCHC MPO and NCDOT agreements for a Congestion Management Process web application (Item 10) and web-based TIP update (Item 11), the November 2018 bid report (Item 12), and Hazard Mitigation Grant Program items (Items 13 and 14). Items 3 and 8 were pulled by resident Victoria Peterson and Item 9 was referred back to staff; the remaining consent items passed 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item 3: Bloomberg Mayor's Challenge Grant
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Victoria Peterson pulled Item 3 and spoke for three minutes, expressing surprise at City Attorney Baker's departure and raising concerns about youth programming and community centers. Mayor Schewel responded that the city operates many community centers open every afternoon serving hundreds of youth and will continue doing so, after which council approved Item 3 by a 7-0 vote.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item 8: First-Time Homebuyer and Economic Development Program Item
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Victoria Peterson pulled Item 8 to critique economic development outreach and highlight violent crime concerns in the community. A council member clarified an acronym referenced during public comment, acknowledged Peterson's concerns about programming, and asked staff to follow up so she is informed about the department's first-time homebuyer and related initiatives, before council voted 7-0 to approve Item 8.

votes.item_title: Refer Agenda Item 9 (Uniformed Unarmed Security Guard Services for City Parking Facilities) Back to Administration
votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Bonfield requested referring Item 9 back to the administration; council moved, seconded, and approved the referral 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 3: Bloomberg Mayor's Challenge Grant
votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Following three minutes of public comment from Victoria Peterson and remarks from Mayor Schewel on afternoon youth services at city community centers, council approved Item 3 unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 8: First-Time Homebuyer and Economic Development Program Item
votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Following public comment from Victoria Peterson and a council member's request for staff follow-up to share program details including first-time homebuyer offerings, council approved Item 8 unanimously 7-0.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Dec 17, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: On December 17, 2018, the Durham City Council approved the consent agenda 7-0 (including a Hyde Amendment repeal resolution and GoTriangle property donation) after pulling Item 6 (CDBG contract with CASA), which passed 7-0 once staff confirmed CASA accepts Section 8 vouchers. Council unanimously approved 7-0 zoning changes for West Point at 751 Revisions 4, the Pinecrest 9.11-acre residential development on the Mary Semans estate (up to 46 units, with a developer-neighborhood agreement for 38 units), Shell Oil at NC 54/Barbee Road, the Ravenstone Conover annexation, and UDO Omnibus Changes 12. Council rejected the Carrington Woods consolidated annexation at 833 Clayton Road (Item 23) by a 3-4 vote—with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Charlie Reece voting Nay—over traffic and pedestrian safety near Southern High School and the absence of a binding development plan. Finally, Council approved UDO text amendment TC18-00006 for private streets (Item 25) by 6-1 votes on both the consistency statement and ordinance, with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and DeDreana Freeman voting Nay (Freeman corrected her initial electronic consistency vote on the record).

agenda_items.title: Announcements, Neighbor Spotlight Award, and Bassett Affair Recognition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson recognized community supporters present for the consent agenda resolution calling for repeal of the Hyde Amendment, and Council Member Charlie Reece noted his and DeDreana Freeman's visit to Reality Cafe. Council presented the Neighbor Spotlight Award to Marianne Kops and heard historical remarks from Ms. Gillespie and Mr. Brown on the 1903 Bassett Affair and 410 Buchanan Boulevard.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Hyde Amendment Repeal Resolution, Legal Aid Eviction Grant, UMD Grant, GoTriangle Donation, Hurricane Florence Grant, Small Wireless Code)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel read consent items covering minutes, RDU Airport and Durham Housing Authority appointments, the Hyde Amendment repeal resolution, Legal Aid of North Carolina eviction defense grant, Urban Ministries of Durham case management grant, GoTriangle light rail property donation, Hurricane Florence mutual aid grant ordinance, and FCC small wireless facility code revisions. Council Member DeDreana Freeman pulled Item 6 (CDBG contract with CASA) to verify Section 8 voucher acceptance, and Council unanimously approved the remaining consent items 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — West Point at 751 Revisions 4
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Jamie Sunyak presented applicant Robert Schonk's request on behalf of Stewart for minor text commitment revisions to an approved Commercial Center (CC-D) plan to add medical office and hospital uses to Building Envelope B (PID 213-146) and prohibit south-facing signage except on Envelopes B and D. The Planning Commission had recommended approval 9-0, and Council adopted both the consistency statement and UDO amendment 7-0 without opposition.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — Pinecrest (1050 West Forest Hills Boulevard)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jamie Sunyak presented Pinecrest Duke LLC's request to rezone 9.11 acres (the estate of Dr. Mary Semans) from RS-20 to PRD 6.00 for up to 46 single-family detached and townhouse units with a 20-foot buffer and 50-foot greenway easement. Applicant representative Ken Spaulding, George Stanziale, Preservation Durham, and Forest Hills neighbors praised 19 community meetings yielding a side agreement to seek a 20% site-plan density reduction to 38 units, while Council Members Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Mark-Anthony Middleton noted the $800,000-$950,000 price points and lamented the applicant's decision not to proffer to Durham Public Schools or the Affordable Housing Fund before approving 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item — CDBG Subrecipient Contract with CASA
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Returning to pulled Item 6, Community Development Director Reginald Johnson confirmed via the Durham Housing Authority and CASA's website that CASA accepts Section 8 vouchers across its properties including Denson, Underwood, and Maplewood. Council Member DeDreana Freeman noted a voucher holder had been told otherwise when calling and urged CASA to train staff accordingly before Council approved the contract 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — Shell Oil Gas Station (1102 NC 54 / Barbee Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jamie Sunyak presented Ash Miller / Quality Oil Company's request to rezone 2.0 acres of a 2.879-acre parcel at NC 54 and Barbee Road from RS-20 and OI to Commercial Neighborhood with a development plan (CN-D) to rebuild the gas station with eight fueling positions. Representative Daniel Dinsbier confirmed dedicating a 35-foot right-of-way and adding sidewalks and a bike lane in response to resident questions, and Council Member Charlie Reece praised removing pumps from the highway right-of-way before passing both motions 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation — Ravenstone Conover (609 Conover Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jamie Sunyak presented a 0.469-acre voluntary annexation, utility extension, and Rural Residential (RR) initial zoning request from John Blackley / Edens Land to combine the parcel with an adjacent city lot for a single house. Staff determined the annexation would be immediately revenue-positive, and Council passed all three motions 7-0 without opposition.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation — Carrington Woods (833 Clayton Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jamie Sunyak presented Glenwood Homes LLC's request for a utility extension, voluntary annexation, and RS-20 to RS-10 rezoning on 8.57 acres near Southern High School without a development plan, which the Planning Commission had voted 2-11 against recommending. Neighbors opposed traffic congestion, pedestrian safety gaps, and lack of a binding lot cap, prompting debate over whether to hold the hearing open for applicant assurances (favored by Jillian Johnson and Steve Schewel) or decide tonight because the applicant declined to file a development plan (urged by Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, and DeDreana Freeman); the annexation ordinance failed 3-4, ending further action.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment — Omnibus Changes 12 (TC18-00002)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Michael Stock presented TC18-00002, containing technical UDO corrections and minor policy updates (excluding Neighborhood Protection Overlay revisions referred back by the Planning Commission), with a January 15, 2019 effective date. Small developer Bill Ripley raised concerns about a 25% cap on two-unit townhouses, changing street node curvature from 75 to 120 degrees, and Cluster Box Unit (CBU) parking mandates; Mayor Schewel noted townhouse restrictions would be revisited under Expanding Housing Choices before Council passed both motions 7-0.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment — Private Streets (TC18-00006)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Michael Stock presented Mitch Craig's (CE Group) privately initiated text amendment to Section 12.2.2 allowing an additional private-street exception primarily in County jurisdiction (already approved by County Commissioners on Nov. 13) while tightening introductory standards requiring private streets to meet or exceed public street standards across City and County. With no public speakers, Council approved the consistency statement and ordinance 6-1, with DeDreana Freeman dissenting on both votes (and correcting her initial electronic consistency vote on the record right after adjournment).

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda (Items 1-4, 5, 7-10, 12-15, excluding pulled Item 6)
votes.discussion_detail: Council approved all consent items except Item 6 (CDBG contract with CASA), which was pulled by DeDreana Freeman to verify whether CASA accepts Section 8 housing vouchers.

votes.item_title: Item 19: Consistency Statement for West Point at 751 Revisions 4 Zoning Map Change
votes.discussion_detail: Following Jamie Sunyak's staff report and brief remarks from applicant Robert Schonk, Council unanimously adopted the consistency statement.

votes.item_title: Item 19: Ordinance Amending the UDO for West Point at 751 Revisions 4
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously approved the text commitment revisions adding medical office/hospital uses to Envelope B and limiting south-facing signage to Envelopes B and D.

votes.item_title: Item 20: Consistency Statement for Pinecrest Zoning Map Change
votes.discussion_detail: After extensive public comment supporting the compromise reached between Pinecrest Duke LLC and Forest Hills neighbors, Council adopted the consistency statement 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 20: Ordinance Amending the UDO for Pinecrest (RS-20 to PRD 6.00)
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously approved rezoning 9.11 acres at 1050 West Forest Hills Boulevard to PRD 6.00 for up to 46 residential units with 19 text commitments and five design commitments.

votes.item_title: Item 6: CDBG Subrecipient Contract Award with CASA
votes.discussion_detail: After Community Development Director Reginald Johnson confirmed CASA accepts Section 8 vouchers across its properties, Council unanimously approved the pulled consent item 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 21: Consistency Statement for Shell Oil Gas Station (1102 NC 54)
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously adopted the consistency statement for the NC 54 and Barbee Road Shell Oil rezoning.

votes.item_title: Item 21: Ordinance Amending the UDO for Shell Oil Gas Station (RS-20/OI to CN-D)
votes.discussion_detail: Council approved rezoning 2.0 acres to Commercial Neighborhood with a development plan for eight fueling positions and 35-foot right-of-way dedication plus sidewalk/bike lane improvements.

votes.item_title: Item 22: Ordinance Annexing Ravenstone Conover (609 Conover Road) and Utility Extension Agreement
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously approved the voluntary annexation and utility extension agreement for 0.469 acres at 609 Conover Road.

votes.item_title: Item 22: Consistency Statement for Ravenstone Conover
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously adopted the consistency statement for the Rural Residential initial zoning of 609 Conover Road.

votes.item_title: Item 22: Ordinance Amending the UDO for Ravenstone Conover Initial Zoning (RR)
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously established Rural Residential zoning effective December 31, 2018 for the annexed Conover Road parcel.

votes.item_title: Item 23: Ordinance Annexing Carrington Woods (833 Clayton Road) and Utility Extension Agreement
votes.notes: Motion failed 3-4; remaining two motions for Item 23 were not taken up.
votes.discussion_detail: Following opposition from neighbors over Southern High School rush-hour traffic, pedestrian safety, and the lack of a binding development plan, the annexation motion failed 3-4 (Middleton, Caballero, Freeman, and Reece voting Nay). Per the City Attorney, the failure of annexation rendered the consistency and RS-10 rezoning motions moot.

votes.item_title: Item 24: Consistency Statement for UDO Text Amendment TC18-00002 (Omnibus Changes 12)
votes.discussion_detail: After public comment from Bill Ripley on townhouse caps, road curvature rules, and mailbox CBU parking, Council unanimously adopted the consistency statement.

votes.item_title: Item 24: Ordinance Adopting UDO Text Amendment TC18-00002 (Omnibus Changes 12, effective Jan 15, 2019)
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously adopted Omnibus Changes 12 with an effective date of January 15, 2019 to align with Durham County Board of Commissioners consideration.

votes.item_title: Item 25: Consistency Statement for UDO Text Amendment TC18-00006 (Private Streets)
votes.notes: Vote tally corrected on the record from 7-0 to 6-1 at 02:52:25 per DeDreana Freeman.
votes.discussion_detail: Initially tallied 7-0 on the electronic voting board, Council Member DeDreana Freeman corrected the record at 02:52:25 to reflect her Nay vote on both the consistency statement and the ordinance.

votes.item_title: Item 25: Ordinance Adopting UDO Text Amendment TC18-00006 (Private Streets)
votes.discussion_detail: Council approved TC18-00006 requiring private streets to meet or exceed public street standards and adding a County private-street allowance, with DeDreana Freeman voting Nay.

disagreements.issue: Carrington Woods (833 Clayton Road) Consolidated Annexation and RS-10 Rezoning Without a Development Plan
disagreements.summary: Council split 3-4 on annexing and rezoning 8.57 acres near Southern High School from RS-20 to RS-10 without a binding development plan, dividing over neighborhood traffic/pedestrian safety concerns, developer accountability, and whether to delay for additional information.
disagreements.side_a_position: Hold the hearing open or approve the annexation/RS-10 rezoning because the modest density increase creates minimal additional traffic beyond by-right development.
side_a_arguments: Transportation staff reported adjacent roads operate below LOS D only in brief 30-minute school rush-hour windows, and adding 7 to 16 lots over by-right RS-20 would not materially worsen traffic.
Holding the public hearing open could let the absent applicant return to provide non-binding assurances on lot count.
disagreements.side_b_position: Decide the case immediately and reject annexation/RS-10 rezoning due to lack of a binding development plan, pedestrian safety gaps, and unequal community treatment.
side_b_arguments: After the Planning Commission delayed two months and voted 2-11 against the project, the applicant still refused to file a development plan locking in lot counts.

Neighborhood residents should not be forced to return a fourth time, and lower-income areas near Southern High School deserve the same developer engagement expected in affluent neighborhoods like Forest Hills.
Unmitigated pedestrian and bus-stop safety gaps along Clayton Road remain unaddressed.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation failed 3-4 at 02:34:30, halting the rezoning.

disagreements.issue: UDO Text Amendment TC18-00006 (Private Streets Standards and County Allowance)
disagreements.summary: While six members approved TC18-00006 to clarify private street certification standards and allow an additional private-street exception primarily in Durham County, DeDreana Freeman dissented on both the consistency statement and ordinance.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the revised text amendment aligning City/County introductory standards and reflecting the County Commissioners' November 13 approval.
side_a_arguments: The applicant substantially narrowed the original proposal after the Planning Commission's 5-7 denial recommendation.
Introductory language strengthens requirements that private streets meet or exceed public street standards.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose the consistency statement and UDO text amendment expanding private street allowances.
side_b_arguments: Cast Nay votes on both the consistency statement and ordinance without extended floor remarks (correcting the electronic record on the consistency vote at 02:52:25).
disagreements.resolution: Both the consistency statement and ordinance passed 6-1.
