meetings.title: Durham City Council June 18, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: With Council Member Javiera Caballero excused absent, the six present Durham City Council members approved the consent agenda 6-0 (including the FY 2018-19 budget, CIP, and fire consolidation with Bethesda and Parkwood) and later passed pulled Item 16 establishing the Racial Equity Task Force 6-0. On Item 31, Council voted 4-2 to remove loose tire mulch at East Durham Park using $20,000 from the General Fund balance rather than delaying Piney Wood soccer field repairs, with Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, DeDreana Freeman, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and Mark-Anthony Middleton and Steve Schewel voting Nay. Council approved street closings for Sycamore Street (Item 44) and Bush Drive (Item 52) by identical 5-1 votes—Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Vernetta Alston in favor, and DeDreana Freeman opposed—while approving Drake Avenue and Sarvis Street closings (Item 51), FY 2018-19 capital facility fees (Item 46), and annexations for 3112 Blue Hill Lane (Item 42) and J.C. Electric (Item 43) unanimously 6-0. Council also kept the public hearing open and continued the Rolling Dale rezoning (Item 45) to August 2018 to obtain a City Attorney ethics review regarding a Planning Commissioner representing the applicant.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Excused Absence, Neighbor Spotlight, and History Lesson
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m., and Council voted 6-0 to grant an excused absence to Council Member Javiera Caballero, who was traveling. Ceremonial items included presenting the Neighbor Spotlight Award to Estella Bell, recognizing the Duke University baseball coaching and support staff, and hearing a local history presentation from public historian Eddie on the 1933 Durham Post Office and Federal Courthouse and the Epps v. Carmichael desegregation case.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1–39, Excluding Item 16, Item 31, and Public Hearings)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read the consent agenda, noting Item 11 (Housing Appeals Board at-large alternate vacancy) was referred back to the City Clerk's office and Item 16 (Racial Equity Task Force) was pulled by a resident for separate consideration. Major items approved on consent included the FY 2018-19 budget, FY 2019-24 Capital Improvement Plan, Council Code of Ethics amendment, sidewalk and utility infrastructure contracts, Durham City-County fire consolidation, and future police headquarters site disposition. Council approved the remaining consent slate 6-0.

agenda_items.title: East Durham Park Tire Mulch Report and Funding Source
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community speakers Lenora Smith and Kristen Henry thanked Council for addressing East Durham Park's tire mulch but criticized Durham Parks and Recreation (DPR) for recommending removal of only the loose tire mulch without consulting residents about remaining bonded tire mulch, urging a systemwide moratorium on recycled tire products. DPR Assistant Director Tom Dawson explained why staff recommended delaying Piney Wood soccer field repairs (a playability rather than safety issue) to pay for removal, which Mark-Anthony Middleton and Steve Schewel supported to protect the General Fund balance. A majority of Council instead backed appropriating $20,000 from fund balance to avoid pitting neighborhoods against one another, passing the motion 4-2.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation for 3112 Blue Hill Lane
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a voluntary annexation and utility extension request for 3112 Blue Hill Lane to allow construction of a city-maintained public street connecting a residential development along Enders Chapel Road to the satellite-annexed Yancy parcel. Applicant representative Charlie Yokley of the McAdams Company attended to answer questions, with no opposition speakers. Council approved the annexation, consistency statement, and initial residential rural zoning in three consecutive 6-0 votes.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation for J.C. Electric Initial (4915 Hillsborough Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a voluntary annexation, utility extension agreement, and initial Industrial Light (IL) zoning request for a 9.9-acre parcel split between Orange and Durham counties under an interlocal annexation agreement with Orange County, intended for an outdoor recreation facility requiring a Board of Adjustment minor special use permit. Council Member Charlie Reece expressed strong frustration with cross-county annexations and assigning IL zoning adjacent to a residential neighborhood, though he voted in favor because of a state-imposed stream buffer. Council approved all three motions 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Sycamore Street Permanent Street Closing (TROSA)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a request by Kimley-Horn on behalf of TROSA to permanently close 465.60 linear feet of an unbuilt, unmaintained paper street segment of Sycamore Street surrounded entirely by TROSA-owned parcels. Proponent representatives Ed Hallberg and Dan Jewell noted the closure is a first step toward future site planning, and opponent Freeman Ledbetter departed after staff addressed his questions before the hearing. Council approved the street closing order 5-1, with DeDreana Freeman voting against.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change for Rolling Dale (602 and 606 West NC Highway 54)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a rezoning request from RS-20 to Planned Development Residential 3.940 for up to 25 townhomes on 6.65 acres, which Planning Commission had recommended approving 9-5. Following extensive public comment and Council questioning over tree buffers and the appearance of conflict from Planning Commissioner Neel Ghosh now representing the developer, Council Members DeDreana Freeman, Charlie Reece, and Mark-Anthony Middleton debated ethics rules and public perception. Per City Attorney guidance that no vote was required, Mayor Schewel kept the public hearing open and continued the item to August 2018 for an ethics review and further developer-neighborhood talks on tree preservation.

agenda_items.title: Ordinance Revising Capital Facility Fees for FY 2018-19
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Don Greeley of the Department of Water Management presented the annual revision to water and sewer capital facility fees (system development fees) prepared with consultant Raftelis to conform to North Carolina General Statutes Chapter 162A Article 8 by the July 1, 2018 statutory deadline. No members of the public spoke during the newly mandated public hearing. Council adopted the fee ordinance 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Drake Avenue and Sarvis Street Permanent Street Closings
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a request associated with Hillandale Partners LLC and adjoining residential property owners to permanently close 157 linear feet of Drake Avenue and 143 linear feet of Sarvis Street (unbuilt paper streets west of Tampa Avenue traversed by a perennial tributary of Ellerbe Creek). Watts Hospital-Hillandale Neighborhood Association representatives Jamie Greener and Tom Miller urged approval to protect the stream topography and coordinate adjacent development off Hillandale Road. Council adopted the permanent closing order 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Bush Drive Permanent Street Closing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a request by Edens Land to permanently close 874 linear feet of unbuilt public right-of-way on Bush Drive as required by a zoning text commitment (Z170014) and site plan condition. Council Member DeDreana Freeman questioned the high number of street closings on the agenda and noted there were several at one meeting. Council passed the closing order 5-1, with DeDreana Freeman voting Nay.

agenda_items.title: Establishment of the City of Durham Racial Equity Task Force (Pulled from Consent)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Chris Tiffany, who pulled Item 16 from the consent agenda, urged Council to allow three-minute public comment periods, appoint task force members directly, and ensure grassroots representation from McDougald Terrace and other majority-minority neighborhoods. Council thanked the City Attorney for drafting the bylaws quickly and adopted the resolution establishing the Racial Equity Task Force 6-0.

votes.discussion_detail: Adopted updated water and sewer system development/capital facility fee schedule conforming to NCGS Chapter 162A Article 8.

votes.discussion_detail: Permanently closed unbuilt paper-street segments of Drake Avenue and Sarvis Street west of Tampa Avenue.

votes.notes: Initially misread as 6-0, immediately corrected to 5-1 with DeDreana Freeman voting No.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved permanent closure of 874 linear feet of unbuilt Bush Drive right-of-way required by zoning case Z170014.

votes.discussion_detail: Approved establishing the City of Durham Racial Equity Task Force following public comment by Chris Tiffany.

disagreements.issue: East Durham Park Tire Mulch Removal Funding Source (General Fund Balance vs. Delaying Piney Wood Soccer Field Repairs)
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-2 over whether to pay $20,000 to remove loose tire mulch at East Durham Park by drawing from the General Fund balance or by following staff's recommendation to delay planned half-penny Parks & Trails repairs to the Piney Wood soccer field for one year.
disagreements.side_a_position: Appropriate $20,000 from General Fund balance so East Durham Park is remediated without delaying Piney Wood or pitting neighborhoods against each other
side_a_arguments: Residents urged not pitting East Durham against another neighborhood's park project
Vernetta Alston noted initial reservations about tapping fund balance but voted Yes to support Council majority for the $20,000 appropriation
disagreements.side_b_position: Follow staff recommendation to delay the Piney Wood soccer field repair by one year instead of tapping General Fund balance
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton argued Piney Wood was a playability/rentability issue rather than a safety hazard and would not be denied, only delayed 12 months
Middleton compared the General Fund balance to a household savings account that should not be raided for a $20,000 project to demonstrate fiscal discipline to taxpayers
disagreements.resolution: Motion to fund loose tire mulch removal via a $20,000 General Fund balance appropriation passed 4-2.

disagreements.issue: Sycamore Street and Bush Drive Permanent Street Closings
disagreements.summary: DeDreana Freeman dissented 5-1 on two permanent street-closing orders (Item 44 Sycamore Street and Item 52 Bush Drive), questioning the high volume of public right-of-way closures coming before Council.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve permanent street-closing orders for unbuilt paper rights-of-way consistent with staff recommendations and prior zoning commitments
side_a_arguments: Both rights-of-way were unbuilt and unmaintained by the city
Staff confirmed Bush Drive closure was required by prior zoning case Z170014 and Sycamore Street was surrounded by TROSA parcels with no agency objections
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose permanent right-of-way closures amid high volume of street closings
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman questioned the unusually large number of street closings appearing on the agenda and voted against closing Sycamore Street and Bush Drive
disagreements.resolution: Both street-closing orders passed 5-1.

disagreements.issue: Rolling Dale Rezoning Ethics Question and Tree Buffer Continuance
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether Planning Commissioner Neel Ghosh representing the Rolling Dale developer after previously participating at the Planning Commission posed a conflict of interest or public perception concern, and how to balance fairness to the attorney with ethics clarity.
disagreements.side_a_position: Continue the public hearing to August 2018 so the City Attorney can review the Code of Ethics facts and the developer can work with neighbors on tree preservation
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece stated that while he did not believe Mr. Ghosh had improper intent, public perception suffers when a Planning Commissioner later represents an applicant before Council
DeDreana Freeman suggested continuing the item and Steve Schewel proposed keeping the public hearing open until August so clear ethics guidance could be obtained
disagreements.side_b_position: Ensure fairness to Mr. Ghosh by clarifying whether any rule actually barred his appearance rather than leaving innuendo
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton pressed the City Attorney for a definitive statement on whether anything was improper and noted uncertainty over whether existing rules even covered the situation
disagreements.resolution: Without objection, Mayor Schewel kept the public hearing open and continued Item 45 to August 2018 for City Attorney ethics review and further developer-neighborhood talks.

meetings.title: Durham City Council June 4, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: All seven members of the Durham City Council met on June 4, 2018, beginning with a 7-0 priority vote referring an employee performance evaluation software contract (Item 19) back to the administration and approving the unpulled consent agenda 7-0. Council held the statutory public hearing on the proposed FY 2018-19 budget and FY 2019-24 Capital Improvement Plan (Item 29), hearing residents advocate for Fayetteville Street corridor investments, eviction diversion funding, city worker flat raises and $15/hour part-time pay, solid waste fleet upgrades, and protected bike lanes. On pulled consent items, Council unanimously approved 7-0 a resolution supporting the National Movement of Congregations of Faith and immigrants in sanctuary (Item 2), Civilian Police Review Board appointments (Item 3), and the Downtown Durham Municipal Service District contract amendment (Item 21), while passing the sale of 700 Canal Street to Copernica Properties LLC (Item 14) 6-1—with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and DeDreana Freeman voting Nay.

agenda_items.title: Announcements, McDougall Terrace Cleanup Recognition, and Referral of Item 19
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Javiera Caballero acknowledged supporters wearing white for Consent Item 2 (resolution supporting immigrants in sanctuary) and explained she would not pull the item so they would not have to wait until the end of the meeting. City Manager Tom Bonfield requested referring Item 19 (software to automate the employee performance evaluation program) back to administration for the next meeting and praised police, fire, Keep Durham Beautiful, and Durham Housing Authority partners for the McDougall Terrace community cleanup day. Council approved referring Item 19 back 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval (Excluding Pulled Items 2, 3, 14, and 21)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read the consent agenda, noting Items 2, 3, 14, and 21 were pulled for separate consideration at the end of the meeting and Item 19 had been referred back to administration. Approved items included the Dependent Eligibility Verification audit, DHA affordable housing contract amendment, Avondale Drive sidewalk and roundabout municipal agreements, downtown transportation study, and Duke University fiber optic partnership agreements. Council approved the remaining consent agenda 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing on Proposed FY 2018-19 Budget and FY 2019-24 CIP
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Bertha Johnson opened the statutory public hearing on the proposed FY 2018-19 budget and FY 2019-24 CIP. Seven speakers testified: Catherine Malloy, Denise Hester, and Larry Hester requested gateway signage, $5 million for streetscape engineering, and $10 million in business/rehab funds for the historic Fayetteville Street corridor; Diane Standaert praised the $200,000 eviction diversion allocation; city employees Max Davis and Sarah Vukalich called for a 3% flat raise, $15/hour pay for seasonal/part-time workers, new solid waste trucks, and compensation study transparency; and Bike Durham chair Landous Meisner urged funding for protected bike lanes and Vision Zero infrastructure. Mayor Schewel closed the public hearing with no vote scheduled until June 18.

agenda_items.title: Resolution in Support of the National Movement of Congregations of Faith (Pulled from Consent)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Multiple speakers, including Lee Mortimer, Chris Tiffany, and sanctuary supporters in white, praised Council Member Javiera Caballero's resolution supporting immigrants facing deportation and congregations providing sanctuary, such as Jose Chicas. Council initially voted 7-0 at 00:47:22 without a formal motion and second on the record, and after City Attorney advice returned to take a formal motion and second, passing the resolution 7-0 at 00:51:40.

agenda_items.title: Appointment of Civilian Police Review Board Members (Pulled from Consent)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Chris Tiffany, who pulled Item 3 from consent, criticized the Civilian Police Review Board (CPRB) as ineffective, alleging complaint-intake failures, one-minute public comment caps, and an incident involving an eight-year-old. Council moved and seconded approval of the CPRB appointments and passed the item 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Proposed Sale of Property at 700 Canal Street to Copernica Properties LLC (Pulled from Consent)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman pulled Item 14 to verify whether General Services and Parks and Recreation had reviewed the 700 Canal Street parcel for potential trail access or trail connectivity. Staff confirmed the review had taken place. On the motion to approve the property sale, Council passed the item 6-1 with DeDreana Freeman voting Nay.

agenda_items.title: FY 2018-19 Amendment to Contract for Downtown Durham Municipal Service District (Pulled from Consent)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman pulled Item 21 to raise racial equity concerns about Exhibit A language calling for electronically tracking 'unusual activity' downtown and asked the City Manager about adding public restrooms downtown to address public urination issues. Staff agreed to provide follow-up information after the meeting. Following brief clarification of the motion wording to approve the amendment, Council approved Item 21 7-0.

votes.item_title: Refer Item 19 (Employee Performance Evaluation Automation Software) Back to Administration
votes.discussion_detail: Council approved City Manager Tom Bonfield's priority request to refer Item 19 back to administration for the next council meeting.

votes.item_title: Approve Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Items 2, 3, 14, and 21)
votes.discussion_detail: Unanimous approval of the remaining consent agenda items after Items 2, 3, 14, and 21 were pulled for separate consideration and Item 19 was referred back.

votes.item_title: Item 3: Approve Appointments of Civilian Police Review Board Members
votes.discussion_detail: Following public criticism from Chris Tiffany regarding CPRB complaint handling, Council unanimously approved the board appointments.

meetings.title: Durham City Council May 21, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: All seven Durham City Council members met for a marathon session featuring City Manager Tom Bonfield's $510.4 million proposed FY 2018-19 budget presentation (with no property tax rate increase) and sharp split votes on participatory budgeting (PB) and water-main rescissions. On Item 4, Council passed PB guidelines 5-2—Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye; Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman voting Nay—and then approved a $2.4 million FY20 PB allocation 5-2, with Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye against Mark-Anthony Middleton and Steve Schewel voting Nay. Council passed the Fayetteville Commercial rezoning (Item 17) 6-1 across three votes (DeDreana Freeman opposed; all other six members in favor), unanimously approved a $250,000 economic incentive grant for Thompson Joinery LLC (Item 18) and Hardwick Drive sidewalk assessments (Item 19) 7-0, and voted 4-3 to rescind previously ordered water mains on Bandock/Rondelay Drive (Item 20) and Olive Branch/Bookman Street (Item 21)—with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and Mark-Anthony Middleton, DeDreana Freeman, and Charlie Reece voting Nay.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Recognitions, Priority Referral of Item 9, and Consent Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council presented ceremonial proclamations for Playball Summer and National Gun Violence Awareness Day and heard announcements including promotion of the Black Enterprise Entrepreneurs Summit. Council voted 7-0 to refer Item 9 (ferric sulfate bid contract) back to administration and approved the consent agenda 7-0, including FY 2018-19 water and sewer rates, the City-County Planning work program, and small wireless facility ordinance revisions.

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Proposed FY 2018-19 Budget and FY 2019-24 CIP Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield presented a proposed $510.4 million total FY 2018-19 budget ($201.1 million General Fund) with no property tax rate increase, funded by 4.46% tax base growth. Highlights included merging the Bethesda and Parkwood county fire districts into the city (53 positions), adding 15 firefighters for a downtown engine company, 9 development services positions funded by fees, $450,000 for homelessness and eviction diversion, 4% general employee and 5% sworn public safety merit pay raises, $300,000 to launch participatory budgeting, and launching a three-year Comprehensive Plan update. No vote was taken, with the public hearing set for June 4.

agenda_items.title: Participatory Budgeting (PB) Guidelines and FY 2020 Funding Allocation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following public comment from James Chavis (criticizing lack of Black community outreach) and Frederick A. Davis II (urging $2 million for shared economic prosperity and minority businesses), Council debated PB guidelines and project funding for FY 2019-20. Council removed the word 'only' from the first-year ward-based district language per Vernetta Alston's suggestion and adopted the guidelines 5-2 over objections from Mark-Anthony Middleton (who warned against launching with flawed ward boundaries) and DeDreana Freeman (who raised racial equity and process concerns). On the FY20 funding amount, Charlie Reece moved $2.4 million (divisible across three districts), which passed 5-2 over opposition from Middleton ($750,000 staff recommendation) and Mayor Schewel ($1 million ceiling), while Freeman voted Yes despite process reservations.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Land Use Item for Fayetteville Commercial (4510 Fayetteville Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a request by Morningstar Law Group on behalf of Yolanda Hall Long and Michael Hall to change the Future Land Use Map and zoning for 2.8 acres at Fayetteville Road and MLK Jr. Parkway from RS-20 to Commercial General without a development plan. Family members and attorney Patrick Byker argued that city road projects left the five-generation family parcel undevelopable for residential use and cited a 300-foot forested stream buffer; opponents raised traffic, noise, and unrestricted CG use concerns. While six members supported granting commercial zoning, DeDreana Freeman argued the lack of development-plan protections or comparative impact tools harmed the surrounding neighborhood and voted No across all three 6-1 votes.

agenda_items.title: Economic Development Incentive Agreement with Thompson Joinery LLC
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chris Dickey of the Office of Economic and Workforce Development presented a $250,000 neighborhood revitalization incentive grant for Thompson Joinery LLC to acquire and renovate the historic Garland Woodcraft site on South Driver Street in East Durham—leveraging $3.8 million in private investment, retaining 26 living-wage jobs, creating 19 new jobs, and activating six retail storefronts. Owner Matt Thompson and supporters spoke on preserving skilled millwork trades and partnering with NCWorks and Durham Tech. Following questioning from Jillian Johnson, DeDreana Freeman, and Javiera Caballero on workforce racial diversity, living wages (starting at $16.50/hour), and hiring justice-involved residents, Council approved the grant 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Confirmation of Sidewalk Assessment Roll on Hardwick Drive
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Robert Joyner of Public Works presented a resolution confirming the sidewalk assessment roll for a portion of Hardwick Drive, noting staff received no objections and one property owner was paying actual cost at 8.25% interest. With no public speakers, Council adopted the resolution 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Rescind Previously Ordered Water Main on Bandock Drive and Rondelay Drive
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Robert Joyner presented staff's recommendation to rescind a long-pending petitioned water main for 43 lots currently served by Aqua, noting a regional sewer pump station project is roughly four years from completion. Resident Mr. Harris opposed rescinding the 2010 unanimous petition, citing lack of fire protection after a house fire, while Mayor Schewel suggested future annexation once sewer becomes available. Council voted 4-3 to rescind the water main, with Mark-Anthony Middleton, DeDreana Freeman, and Charlie Reece voting Nay.

agenda_items.title: Rescind Previously Ordered Water Main on Olive Branch Road and Bookman Street
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Robert Joyner presented staff's recommendation to rescind a 2010 petitioned water main serving Olive Branch Road and Bookman Street, noting Olive Branch Baptist Church submitted a letter stating its well is failing. Church representative Todd Wright urged Council to keep the project active, offering right-of-way dedication and voluntary annexation. Council nevertheless voted 4-3 to rescind the order, with Mark-Anthony Middleton, DeDreana Freeman, and Charlie Reece again voting Nay.

votes.item_title: Refer Item 9 (Ferric Sulfate 13% Bid Contract) Back to Administration
votes.discussion_detail: Approved City Manager Tom Bonfield's priority item referring Item 9 back to administration.

votes.item_title: Item 4 (Motion 1): Adopt Participatory Budgeting Guidelines as Amended
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman voted No.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted PB guidelines with Vernetta Alston's amendment removing 'only' from the geographic boundaries first-year ward clause.

votes.item_title: Item 4 (Motion 2): Allocate $2.4 Million for FY 2019-20 Participatory Budgeting Projects
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved allocating $2.4 million in FY 2019-20 ($800,000 per ward/district) for PB projects; passed 5-2 over opposition from Mark-Anthony Middleton (who favored $750,000) and Steve Schewel (who favored $1 million).

votes.item_title: Item 17 (Motion 1): Amend Future Land Use Map to Commercial for 4510 Fayetteville Road
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman announced she would vote against prior to the motion.
votes.discussion_detail: Amended FLUM designation for 4510 Fayetteville Road from Low Density Residential to Commercial.

votes.item_title: Item 17 (Motion 2): Adopt Consistency Statement for Fayetteville Commercial
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman voted No.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted statutory consistency statement for 4510 Fayetteville Road rezoning.

votes.item_title: Item 17 (Motion 3): Adopt UDO Amendment Rezoning 4510 Fayetteville Road from RS-20 to Commercial General (CG)
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman voted No.
votes.discussion_detail: Rezoned 2.8 acres at 4510 Fayetteville Road to Commercial General without a development plan.

votes.item_title: Item 18: Authorize Economic Development Incentive Agreement ($250,000) with Thompson Joinery LLC
votes.discussion_detail: Authorized the City Manager to execute a $250,000 neighborhood revitalization grant agreement with Thompson Joinery LLC for the Garland Woodcraft complex on South Driver Street.

votes.item_title: Item 19: Adopt Resolution Confirming Sidewalk Assessment Roll on Hardwick Drive
votes.discussion_detail: Confirmed the sidewalk assessment roll for a portion of Hardwick Drive.

votes.item_title: Item 20: Adopt Resolution Rescinding Previously Ordered Water Main on Bandock Drive and Rondelay Drive
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton, DeDreana Freeman, and Charlie Reece voted No.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted staff's recommendation to rescind the 2010 petitioned water main improvement serving Bandock Drive and Rondelay Drive.

votes.item_title: Item 21: Adopt Resolution Rescinding Previously Ordered Water Main on Olive Branch Road and Bookman Street
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton, DeDreana Freeman, and Charlie Reece voted No.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted staff's recommendation to rescind the 2010 petitioned water main improvement serving Olive Branch Road and Bookman Street despite Olive Branch Baptist Church's failing well.

disagreements.issue: Participatory Budgeting (PB) Guidelines and Ward-Based Process
disagreements.summary: Council split 5-2 on adopting PB guidelines that initially organized the process by Durham's three wards, with Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman objecting to process transparency, racial equity safeguards, and ward structure.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt the committee-crafted PB guidelines with flexibility to adjust ward boundaries after year one
side_a_arguments: Guidelines reflected extensive work-session compromise led by Javiera Caballero, Vernetta Alston, and DeDreana Freeman
Removing 'only' from the first-year ward clause prevented boxing Council into an immediate guideline amendment while keeping the launch on schedule
disagreements.side_b_position: Delay or revise the guidelines to fix structural ward inequities, transparency, and racial equity criteria before launching
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton objected to proceeding with ward boundaries that colleagues already acknowledged were structurally problematic just to meet a timeline
DeDreana Freeman argued the process lacked clear racial equity benchmarks and adequate outreach to Black and low-income communities
disagreements.resolution: PB guidelines passed 5-2.

disagreements.issue: Participatory Budgeting FY 2020 Funding Amount ($2.4M vs. $750K–$1M)
disagreements.summary: Council split 5-2 over how much FY 2019-20 capital/project funding to commit to participatory budgeting, pitting a $2.4 million coalition against fiscal incrementalism favored by Mark-Anthony Middleton ($750,000) and Steve Schewel ($1 million).
disagreements.side_a_position: Allocate $2.4 million ($800,000 per ward) to make PB projects meaningful and drive broad resident participation
side_a_arguments: Jillian Johnson cited the national best practice of $1M per 100,000 residents and strong fund balance reserves that avoid tax hikes
Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, and Vernetta Alston argued a substantial pot enables residents—including non-voters—to propose impactful neighborhood projects
DeDreana Freeman voted Yes while pledging strict vigilance on racial equity and people-of-color representation
disagreements.side_b_position: Start with the staff-recommended $750,000 (Middleton) or at most $1 million (Schewel) in year one and scale up later
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton urged incrementalism aligned with staff's $750,000 recommendation so more dollars stay focused on housing eviction diversion, jobs, and justice-involved residents
Steve Schewel supported PB strongly but considered $1 million sufficient for a first-year pilot before scaling
disagreements.resolution: Motion allocating $2.4 million for FY 2019-20 PB projects passed 5-2.

disagreements.issue: Fayetteville Commercial Rezoning Without a Development Plan (4510 Fayetteville Road)
disagreements.summary: DeDreana Freeman dissented 6-1 on rezoning 4510 Fayetteville Road to Commercial General without a development plan, contrasting neighborhood-impact concerns against the Hall family's loss of residential viability after MLK Parkway construction.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the FLUM amendment and Commercial General rezoning for 4510 Fayetteville Road
side_a_arguments: City road projects (MLK Jr. Parkway and Fayetteville Road improvements) rendered the five-generation family parcel undevelopable for residential use and restricted to right-in/right-out access
A 300-foot preserved forested stream valley buffers nearby Hanson Road homes
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose open-ended Commercial General rezoning without development-plan restrictions or neighborhood impact tracking
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman noted Council lacked adequate tools to measure neighborhood impacts or restrict future uses without a development plan, making it difficult to favor one property owner over surrounding residents
disagreements.resolution: All three motions for 4510 Fayetteville Road passed 6-1.

disagreements.issue: Rescinding 2010 Petitioned Water Mains on Bandock/Rondelay Drive and Olive Branch/Bookman Street
disagreements.summary: Council divided 4-3 on rescinding two 2010 petitioned water mains outside city limits, weighing cost and future annexation/sewer plans against residents' fire-safety concerns and Olive Branch Baptist Church's failing well.
disagreements.side_a_position: Rescind the old petitioned water main orders per Public Works recommendation
side_a_arguments: Bandock/Rondelay residents already receive water from Aqua and could pursue annexation in roughly four years when a regional sewer pump station is completed
Rescinding avoids high city construction costs under outdated 2010 petition rates
disagreements.side_b_position: Vote against rescinding and honor the 2010 utility orders
side_b_arguments: Residents on Bandock/Rondelay cited lack of fire hydrants and fire protection, and Olive Branch Baptist Church reported a failing well and offered voluntary annexation and right-of-way dedication
disagreements.resolution: Both rescission resolutions passed 4-3.

meetings.title: Durham City Council May 7, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: All seven members of the Durham City Council approved referring duplicate February 5 meeting minutes back (7-0) and passed the consent agenda 7-0 before hearing annual reports from the Durham Youth Commission (Item 14) and Police Chief C.J. Davis's first-quarter 2018 crime report (Item 15). Following a nearly two-and-a-half-hour public hearing on the Old West Durham Neighborhood Protection Overlay (Item 16, TC180001 and Z180002), Council unanimously voted 7-0 across four motions to adopt the overlay—capping primary home size and height, requiring backyard trees, and permitting 800-square-foot accessory dwelling units (ADUs). On two public hearings to rescind previously ordered 2007/2010 petitioned water mains along Stallings Road (Items 17 and 18), Council voted 3-4 against staff's rescission recommendations, keeping the water main projects active: Vernetta Alston, Steve Schewel, and Jillian Johnson voted Aye to rescind, while Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Mark-Anthony Middleton voted Nay.

agenda_items.title: Water Poster Awards, Priority Minutes Referral, and Consent Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel recognized student winners of the state and local water conservation poster contest, and Council heard announcements including a shout-out to Malcolm X's birthday by DeDreana Freeman. Per the City Clerk's priority request to remove duplicated February 5 minutes from Item 1, Council voted 7-0 to refer them back, and then approved the consent agenda 7-0 (including a Durham County sales-tax sharing interlocal agreement, HOPWA and CDBG homelessness contracts, and the Bloomberg Mayors Challenge grant).

agenda_items.title: 2017–2018 Durham Youth Commission Annual Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Durham Youth Commission officers and presenters Natalie Perkins (Hillside High School) and Jessica Uba (City of Medicine Academy) presented an overview of the Commission's 2017-18 service year and youth policy engagement activities. No Council vote was taken.

agenda_items.title: First Quarter 2018 Crime Report Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief C.J. Davis and Assistant Chief Marsh responded to Council questions on the Q1 2018 crime report, highlighting crime-reduction trends in Districts 1 and 4, take-home patrol vehicle visibility, high clearance rates, and felony/juvenile petition procedures after Jillian Johnson questioned an eight-year-old's vandalism citation. Mark-Anthony Middleton publicly thanked Chief Davis for her integrity amid external criticism following Council's April 16 international police exchanges statement, and Mayor Schewel noted reduced misdemeanor diversion referrals and CIT outreach during March prostitution arrests. No formal vote was taken.

agenda_items.title: Old West Durham Neighborhood Protection Overlay (TC180001 & Z180002)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Matthew Filter presented the Old West Durham Neighborhood Association's proposed Neighborhood Protection Overlay covering 428 one- and two-family parcels, including a late OWDNA revision raising the ADU cap from 700 to 800 square feet; Planning Commission had recommended denial 5-4. After over two hours of polarized resident and property-owner testimony regarding infill scale, tree canopy, property rights, and housing affordability, all seven Council members endorsed the overlay—citing ADU permissions, stormwater/impervious limits, a 32.5% FAR cap already met by 94% of homes, and citizen-led neighborhood preservation—passing all four consistency and ordinance motions 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Rescind Previously Ordered Water Main on Stallings Road South of Mineral Springs Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works staff Robert Joyner recommended rescinding an 11-year-old petitioned water main on Stallings Road south of Mineral Springs Road. Resident Teresa Price testified she had followed the city's 2007 petition process, granted an easement, and paid roughly $6,000 in assessment fees plus a property lien while waiting 11 years for construction, and Vernon Allen urged Council not to abandon remaining residents. Despite discussion of updated city policy favoring developer-style full-cost construction, a 3-4 vote defeated the rescission motion, leaving Option 1 (moving forward with the water main) in effect.

agenda_items.title: Rescind Previously Ordered Water Main on Stallings Road South of Oak Grove Parkway
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works staff Robert Joyner recommended rescinding the companion petitioned water main on Stallings Road south of Oak Grove Parkway. With no public speakers signed up and Council noting the same policy considerations as Item 17, the motion to rescind failed by an identical 3-4 vote, with Vernetta Alston, Steve Schewel, and Jillian Johnson voting Yes to rescind and the remaining four members voting No.

votes.item_title: Refer Duplicated February 5 Council Minutes in Consent Item 1 Back to Clerk
votes.discussion_detail: Approved the City Clerk's priority request to remove duplicated February 5 minutes from Consent Item 1.

votes.notes: Clerk initially misread 6-0, immediately corrected to 7-0.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted statutory consistency statement for Old West Durham NPO text amendment TC180001.

votes.item_title: Item 16 (Motion 2): Adopt UDO Text Amendment Establishing Old West Durham NPO Standards (TC180001)
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted UDO Article 4 text revisions creating Old West Durham NPO rules (including 800 sq ft ADU cap, 32.5% FAR, height limits, and backyard tree requirement).

meetings.title: Durham City Council Apr 16, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: With Council Member Vernetta Alston excused absent due to a flight delay, the six present Durham City Council members unanimously adopted 6-0 a high-profile policy statement endorsing Police Chief C.J. Davis's commitment against police exchanges with Israel and opposing international exchanges involving military-style training, following testimony from roughly 50 speakers. Council also heard a historic bilingual English-Spanish statement from Javiera Caballero and Steve Schewel condemning recent ICE apartment raids, approved the consent agenda (including the Downtown Master Plan update) 6-0, and adopted the FY 2018-19 Annual Action Plan (Item 26) and Design District streetscape text amendment (Item 21) 6-0. On land use, DeDreana Freeman cast sole dissents as Council passed the Lumley Road rezoning (Item 22) 5-1, the Crutchfield Street consistency statement (Item 23) 5-1 (while passing the FLUM and zoning 6-0), and the 3404 Page Road annexation and rezoning for 190 townhomes (Item 25) 5-1 across four votes—with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, and Mark-Anthony Middleton voting Aye. Late in the five-hour session, Council voted 2-4 against rescinding previously ordered sewer mains on Red Coach/Grand Oaks Roads (Item 27) and East Geer Street (Item 28), keeping both sewer projects alive as Steve Schewel and Jillian Johnson voted Aye to rescind while Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Mark-Anthony Middleton voted Nay.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absence, Proclamations, Priority Referral of Item 16, and Consent Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 6-0 to grant an excused absence to Vernetta Alston due to a flight delay (she was absent throughout the meeting). Ceremonial items honored the MEAC champion NCCU men's basketball team, Spring Valley Elementary third-graders reciting their daily affirmation pledge, and Sunday Supper Durham against food insecurity. Council voted 6-0 to refer Item 16 (Miracle League utility extension agreement) back to administration and approved the consent agenda 6-0, including adopting the Downtown Master Plan updates (Item 19).

agenda_items.title: Bilingual Statement on April 12 ICE Arrests and Council Statement on International Police Exchanges
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Javiera Caballero (delivering Council's first speech in Spanish from the podium) and Steve Schewel presented a joint statement recounting and condemning an April 12 ICE raid on a Durham apartment complex. Council then turned to its draft statement on International Police Exchanges, followed by roughly 50 speakers debating Jewish Voice for Peace's petition, Durham's policing reforms, and community accusations from both Jewish Voice for Peace and Voices for Israel. Mayor Schewel defended Chief C.J. Davis's record of dramatic drops in traffic stops, searches, and drug charges, rejected claims that DPD trained with the Israeli military or that Council's statement attacked Israel unfairly, and Council adopted the statement barring military-style international police exchanges 6-0.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment TC170007: Design District Streetscape Alternatives
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Michael Stock presented privately initiated text amendment TC170007 (submitted by Tim Summerly of Stewart LLC) allowing alternative streetscape standards for contiguous Design District plans of at least 10 acres with property-owner maintenance agreements. Both Planning Commission (14-0) and JCCPC endorsed the measure, and applicants Tim Summerly and George Stanziale stood by for questions. Council adopted the consistency statement and ordinance 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change for Lumley Road Assemblage (4138 Lumley Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jacob Wiggins presented a request by Andrew Porter and attorney Neel Ghosh (Morningstar Law Group) on behalf of Darlington Advisors to rezone four parcels totaling eight acres at 4138 Lumley Road from Residential Rural to Office and Institutional (OI) without a development plan, matching the FLUM designation and serving as a transition between Industrial Light and residential properties. Planning Commission recommended approval 13-0. Council approved the consistency statement 6-0, while DeDreana Freeman questioned the lack of a development plan and cast the lone Nay vote as the zoning ordinance passed 5-1.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Land Use Item for 410 and 492 Crutchfield Street
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jacob Wiggins presented Kim Griffin Jr.'s request to change 1.7 acres at 410 and 492 Crutchfield Street from RU-5/Medium-High Density Residential to Office/OI without a development plan (clarifying Planning Commission actually approved 8-6 despite a memo typo). Council Member Charlie Reece noted landscape architect Dan Jewell's analysis showing UDO setbacks and parking cap building size at roughly 33,000 square feet, while DeDreana Freeman criticized piecemeal rezonings without a development plan and voted No on the consistency statement to signal support for comprehensive planning reform. Council approved the FLUM amendment 6-0, consistency statement 5-1, and zoning ordinance 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Land Use Item for 3718 North Roxboro Street
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jamie Sunyak presented a request by WithersRavenel to amend the FLUM from Office to Commercial and rezone 1.28 acres at 3718 North Roxboro Street from OI to Commercial Neighborhood with a development plan (CN(D)) capping building size at 20,000 square feet, prohibiting recreation and primary alcohol-retail uses, and adding a bus pull-out and shelter. Planning Commission recommended approval 14-0, and nearby resident Andrew George spoke in favor of redeveloping the trash-strewn lot. Council adopted all three motions 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation for 3404 Page Road (190 Townhomes)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jamie Sunyak presented Stewart Inc. and Shenandoah Homes' request for annexation, utility extension, FLUM amendment (from Industrial to Low-Medium Density Residential), and rezoning from RR to PDR 5.78 for up to 190 townhomes priced around $250,000 on 32.87 acres at 3404 Page Road (Planning Commission approved 10-0). Applicant Robert Schunk and Jeff Palmer proffered a $35,000 affordable housing fund contribution and $500 per added student for DPS, but DeDreana Freeman called $35,000 insufficient ('kind of an insult') when none of the units were affordable at 60% AMI and Page Road traffic was rising. Council passed all four motions 5-1 with Freeman voting Nay.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing and Approval of Draft FY 2018-19 Annual Action Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development staff presented the draft FY 2018-19 Annual Action Plan programming anticipated federal HUD entitlements ($1.8M CDBG, $800K HOME, $165K ESG, $328K HOPWA). Mayor Schewel and DeDreana Freeman questioned staff on Southside Section 108 loan repayments, Beaman Place single-family home RFP plans, $367,000 in HOME housing rehab, and potential OEWD apprenticeship links. Council approved the Annual Action Plan 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Rescind Previously Ordered Sewer Main and Outfall for Red Coach Road and Grand Oaks Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works staff Robert Joyner recommended rescinding a 2007 petitioned sewer main and outfall serving Red Coach Road and Grand Oaks Road. Residents including Darian Raposa, Kelly King, and Terry Jones, along with NC Utilities Commission Public Staff representative David Furr, urged Council to honor the 2007 commitment to resolve failing septic and raw sewage issues. While Steve Schewel and Jillian Johnson voted Yes to rescind based on updated cost/legal criteria, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Mark-Anthony Middleton sided with residents' moral obligation argument, defeating rescission 2-4.

agenda_items.title: Rescind Previously Ordered Sewer Main for East Geer Street
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works staff Robert Joyner presented the companion recommendation to rescind a previously ordered sewer main serving a portion of East Geer Street (noting pre-NCDOT estimate of $545,000). Without objection to closing the hearing after staff questions, Council defeated the rescission motion by an identical 2-4 vote, with Steve Schewel and Jillian Johnson voting Yes and Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Mark-Anthony Middleton voting No.

disagreements.issue: Piecemeal Rezonings Without Development Plans (Items 22 and 23)
disagreements.summary: DeDreana Freeman cast 5-1 dissents on the Lumley Road zoning ordinance and the Crutchfield Street consistency statement to protest approving speculative rezonings without binding development plans or comprehensive-plan alignment.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the Lumley Road and Crutchfield Street Office/OI rezonings
side_a_arguments: Both sites matched or transitioned cleanly with surrounding OI/industrial zoning
Charlie Reece noted Dan Jewell's UDO analysis confirmed Crutchfield Street setbacks and parking constrained building scale to ~33,000 sq ft even without a development plan
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose piecemeal rezonings lacking development plans or comprehensive-plan updates
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman argued approving rezonings without a developer or development plan represents a harmful piecemeal approach that undermines neighborhood planning
disagreements.resolution: Lumley Road passed 5-1; Crutchfield Street consistency passed 5-1 (with FLUM and zoning passing 6-0).

disagreements.issue: 3404 Page Road Townhome Rezoning and Affordable Housing Proffer (Item 25)
disagreements.summary: DeDreana Freeman voted 5-1 against annexing and rezoning 3404 Page Road for 190 market-rate townhomes, calling the developer's $35,000 affordable housing contribution insufficient when zero units were affordable at 60% AMI.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the 3404 Page Road annexation, FLUM change from Industrial, and PDR 5.78 rezoning with proffered $35,000 housing and $500/student school contributions
side_a_arguments: Planning staff noted surrounding Page Road parcels were already residential and not prime industrial land
Developer proffered landscape buffers, turn lanes, $500 per added DPS student, and $35,000 to the affordable housing fund above legal requirements
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose the rezoning over inadequate affordable housing proffers and Page Road traffic
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman noted none of the ~$250,000 townhomes would be affordable at 60% AMI or below and called the $35,000 proffer an insult compared with prior $25,000-per-100-unit benchmarks, while also raising Page Road congestion concerns
disagreements.resolution: All four motions for 3404 Page Road passed 5-1.

disagreements.issue: Rescinding 2007/Previously Ordered Sewer Mains on Red Coach/Grand Oaks and East Geer Street (Items 27 and 28)
disagreements.summary: Council split 2-4 to reject staff's recommendations to rescind previously ordered sewer mains for Red Coach/Grand Oaks Roads and East Geer Street, prioritizing the city's 2007 moral commitment and public health over staff's cost concerns.
disagreements.side_a_position: Rescind the old petitioned sewer main orders
side_a_arguments: Staff noted the 2007 resolution had no set timeline, was not a binding legal obligation, and faced steep cost escalation
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject rescission and fulfill the city's 2007 sewer commitment to residents
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton and Charlie Reece emphasized the city had a moral obligation after a decade of delay while raw sewage and failing septic systems threatened residents and creeks
NC Utilities Commission Public Staff and residents urged moving forward to solve a looming environmental problem and add sewer customers
disagreements.resolution: Both rescission motions failed 2-4, keeping the Red Coach/Grand Oaks and East Geer Street sewer projects active.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Apr 2, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: All seven members of the Durham City Council met on April 2, 2018, issuing proclamations for National Fair Housing Month, the Mayor's Challenge for Water Conservation, National Service Recognition, National Community Development Week, and Crime Victims' Rights Week. Council unanimously approved 7-0 the consent agenda—which included the FY 2018-19 budget development guidelines, General Fund balance policy, Golden Belt office leases, and a resolution supporting public employees' collective bargaining rights—confirming the vote by voice after a brief electronic voting system glitch. Following a public hearing with no speakers, Council voted 7-0 on Item 18 to authorize up to $150 million in limited obligation bonds under an installment finance contract. The remainder of the meeting featured Police Chief C.J. Davis and Analytical Services Manager Jason Schiess presenting the 2017 Fourth Quarter and Annual Crime Report and Traffic Stop Report, documenting a 49% multi-year drop in property crime and steep declines in traffic stops and consent searches while Council pressed for further reductions in racial disparities and minor equipment stops.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations for Fair Housing, Water Conservation, Community Development, and Crime Victims' Rights
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council presented five ceremonial proclamations: National Fair Housing Month (recognizing Human Relations Manager James Davis and the Uneven Ground exhibit), the National Mayor's Challenge for Water Conservation (with Wayne Drop and James Lim), National Service Recognition, National Community Development Week (recognizing Citizens Advisory Committee volunteers), and Crime Victims' Rights Week (with Chief C.J. Davis).

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (FY18-19 Budget Guidelines, Golden Belt Leases, Collective Bargaining Resolution)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With no priority items from the City Manager, Attorney, or Clerk, Council approved the consent agenda 7-0, including FY 2018-19 budget development guidelines, General Fund and Water/Sewer reserve policies, Golden Belt leases for Community Development and NIS, street and stormwater contracts, and Item 20 supporting public employees' collective bargaining rights. When the electronic voting display malfunctioned briefly, Council re-confirmed the 7-0 consent vote unanimously by voice.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing and Resolution Authorizing Up to $150 Million in Limited Obligation Bonds
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Treasury Manager Emily Desiderio presented a resolution approving an installment finance contract and authorizing limited obligation bonds not to exceed $150 million, previously reviewed at Council's budget retreat. No members of the public spoke during the public hearing, and Council adopted the bond authorization 7-0.

agenda_items.title: 2017 Fourth Quarter / Annual Crime Report and Traffic Stop Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief C.J. Davis reported that violent crime rose slightly by 7 incidents in 2017 (with reported rapes up 28% largely due to 19 belated reports amid the #MeToo movement) while long-term violent crime dropped 11% and property crime fell 49%, alongside expanded PAL mentoring and pre-hire recruiting. Analytical Services Manager Jason Schiess presented the 2017 traffic stop report showing consent search rates falling below 0.5% across racial groups from 2013 to 2017. Council members praised the cultural shift while urging reductions in remaining Black-white search disparities and minor equipment-violation stops affecting undocumented residents, with no vote taken.

votes.item_title: Item 18: Adopt Resolution Approving Installment Finance Contract and Limited Obligation Bonds (Up to $150M)
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted resolution authorizing limited obligation bonds up to $150 million following a public hearing with no speakers.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Mar 19, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: With Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton excused absent due to an out-of-state flight mechanical delay, the six present Durham City Council members conducted all business unanimously by 6-0 votes. Council approved the consent agenda 6-0 (with the 2017 annual crime report deferred to April 2) and held a public hearing on the upcoming FY 2018-19 budget and FY 2019-24 CIP (Item 15), where UE 150 city workers testified on aging, unsafe public works and water management trucks, flat $2,500 raises, $15/hour part-time pay, and arts compensation. Council then unanimously approved three development items in three 6-0 blocks: revisions to non-residential design commitments for Arringdon II (Item 16, 2 votes), a plan amendment and rezoning for 50 townhomes in Page Park II (Item 17, 3 votes), and a plan amendment and rezoning for a Volvo dealership at Park at South Point II (Item 18, 3 votes).

agenda_items.title: Excused Absence, Neighbor Spotlight, CROP Walk Proclamation, and Consent Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Charlie Reece moved and Council voted 6-0 to grant an excused absence to Mark-Anthony Middleton, who was stranded out of state by a broken airplane. Council presented the March Neighbor Spotlight to Constance Wright for Red Maple Park and proclaimed March 25 as Durham CROP Hunger Walk Day (in memory of Chuck Davis). After the City Manager noted Item 14 (2017 crime report) was deferred until April 2, Council approved the consent agenda 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing on FY 2018-19 Budget and FY 2019-24 Capital Improvement Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Bertha Johnson opened the pre-budget public hearing ahead of the May 21 budget presentation, June 4 hearing, and June 18 adoption. Six speakers addressed Council, including UE 150 stewards and city employees Daryl Brunson, Romy Gaddy, and Donald Quick—who cited aging 2003–2005 trucks breaking down in Water Management and Public Works, rising healthcare costs, merit-pay grievances, a demand for $2,500 across-the-board raises, and $15/hour pay for part-time and temporary workers—alongside artist Monica Byrne urging fair compensation for independent artists. No vote was taken.

agenda_items.title: Revisions to Design Commitments for Arringdon II (Z090015)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jamie Sunyak presented Jonathan Parsons' (J. Davis) request to clarify design commitment text for non-residential buildings and signs in the 95.6-acre Arringdon II mixed-use development east of Page Road without altering the overall development plan. Planning Commission recommended approval 10-0. Council adopted the consistency statement and zoning ordinance 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Item for Page Park II (4801 Crown Parkway, 50 Townhomes)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jamie Sunyak presented Stewart Inc.'s request on behalf of Lennar to amend the FLUM from Commercial to Low-Medium Density Residential and rezone Tract B at 4801 Crown Parkway to RSMD for 50 townhomes (priced around $200,000–$225,000) instead of 29,100 sq ft of retail (Planning Commission recommended approval 13-0). Javiera Caballero questioned BPAC's crosswalk and bike-lane comments (staff confirmed a crosswalk at site plan and an existing 14-foot outside lane), and Mayor Schewel noted the developer's DPS school proffer and urged builders to bring ideas on affordable housing. Council adopted all three motions 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change for Park at South Point II (Southpoint Auto Park Boulevard)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jacob Wiggins presented Robert Schunk and attorney Ken Spaulding's request across nine parcels along Southpoint Auto Park Boulevard to amend the FLUM to Commercial and rezone to Commercial General with a development plan (CG(D)) for up to 55,000 sq ft of auto sales (a Volvo dealership), prohibiting outdoor paging systems and limiting impervious surface to 70% (Planning Commission approved 10-0). DeDreana Freeman questioned why landscaping standards differed from nearby Hendrick Southpoint, and staff agreed to provide a list of ordinance changes. Council adopted all three motions 6-0.

meetings.title: Durham City Council March 5, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: All seven members of the Durham City Council met on March 5, 2018, issuing proclamations for Girl Scout Week and Women's History Month and swearing in inaugural members of the Mayor's Council for Women. Council approved the consent agenda (excluding pulled Item 16) 7-0, adopting the Durham Sustainability Roadmap, transit vehicle replacements, and external auditor selection, and later approved pulled Item 16 (Spirit Communications telecommunications license) 7-0 after DeDreana Freeman commended the company for sharing workforce diversity statistics. Council unanimously approved 7-0 a consolidated annexation and rezoning for 79 townhomes at 5220 Wake Forest Highway (Item 19, 4 votes) and the permanent street closing of Rent Road for Ellis Road Phase II (Item 20). On Item 21 (NC 54 Storage at 1003 East NC Highway 54), Council unanimously approved the FLUM amendment and consistency statement 7-0 before passing the Commercial General zoning ordinance 6-1—with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and DeDreana Freeman voting Nay over downstream stormwater flooding concerns.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations, Consent Agenda Approval, and Swearing-In of Mayor's Council for Women
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Girl Scout Troop 998 and Cub Scout Troop 424 led the Pledge of Allegiance, followed by proclamations for Girl Scout Week and Women's History Month (honoring Jean Bradley Anderson). Council approved the consent agenda 7-0 (with Item 16 pulled by DeDreana Freeman for a brief question), adopting the Durham Sustainability Roadmap, transit radio and vehicle replacements, and external auditor selection, and then swore in inaugural members of the Mayor's Council for Women.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation for 5220 Wake Forest Highway (79 Townhomes)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jamie Sunyak presented Eastwood Homes of Raleigh LLC's request for voluntary annexation, utility extension agreement, FLUM amendment (Low to Low-Medium Density Residential), and rezoning to PDR 5.362 for up to 79 townhomes on 14.919 acres at 5220 Wake Forest Highway (Planning Commission approved 8-4). Commitments included a 50-foot southern setback, enhanced tree coverage, and bike-lane asphalt. Council adopted all four motions unanimously 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Rent Road Permanent Street Closing (896 Linear Feet)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jamie Sunyak presented Ellis Road Residential LP's request to permanently close 896 linear feet of Rent Road right-of-way to conform with the approved Ellis Road Phase II site plan (D1400380). Answering DeDreana Freeman's concern about converting public streets to private property without a fee, staff clarified that a new, realigned public road was replacing the closed segment. Council approved the street closing order 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Land Use Item for NC 54 Storage (1003 East NC Highway 54)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jamie Sunyak presented a request to amend the FLUM from Office to Commercial and rezone 1.9 acres at 1003 East NC 54 from RS-20 to CG(D) for a 120,000-square-foot self-storage facility with a bus pull-out, bike-lane right-of-way, and cross-access easement (Planning Commission approved 8-4). DeDreana Freeman questioned Public Works staff Robert Joyner extensively about downstream stormwater runoff and potential flooding at nearby apartments, while Mayor Schewel suggested a stormwater facility tour for new council members. Council passed the FLUM amendment and consistency statement 7-0, and passed the zoning ordinance 6-1 with Freeman voting Nay.

agenda_items.title: Telecommunications License Agreement with Spirit Communications (Pulled from Consent)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Returning to pulled Consent Item 16, DeDreana Freeman thanked South Carolina Telecommunications Group LLC (d/b/a Spirit Communications) for voluntarily sharing its workforce diversity statistics and engaging in constructive conversation on diversity as a small business. Council approved the telecommunications license agreement 7-0.

disagreements.issue: Downstream Stormwater Flooding Concerns on NC 54 Storage Rezoning (Item 21)
disagreements.summary: DeDreana Freeman cast the sole dissent (6-1) on the CG(D) zoning ordinance for NC 54 Storage after questioning whether stormwater detention elongation could worsen downstream flooding near neighboring apartments.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the NC 54 Storage CG(D) rezoning relying on city stormwater detention and inspection standards
side_a_arguments: Public Works staff Robert Joyner explained stormwater impact analysis requires detention back to pre-development flow rates (up to 100-year storm events when downstream flooding exists)
Steve Schewel noted stormwater ponds are inspected annually and the city cannot ban uphill development solely on general proximity, proposing a stormwater tour for new members

meetings.title: Durham City Council Feb 19, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: All seven members of the Durham City Council met on February 19, 2018 and conducted every vote unanimously 7-0. After approving the consent agenda 7-0 (including transit grant ordinances, Birchwood Park and American Tobacco Trail parking contracts, and a watershed protection plan), Council amended City Noise Ordinance Section 26-23 (Item 14) on a 7-0 motion by Charlie Reece to extend the Durham Central Park sound exception from 8:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m. for groups such as Batalá Durham, before adopting the revised ordinance 7-0 and referring broader complaint-driven noise enforcement citywide to the Environmental Affairs Board. Council then unanimously adopted three Unified Development Ordinance text amendments in paired 7-0 consistency and ordinance votes: Omnibus 11 technical revisions (Item 10, TC170005), state-mandated sedimentation and erosion control updates (Item 11, TC170006, which Jillian Johnson criticized as General Assembly preemption weakening local environmental protections), and the landmark Compact Neighborhood Interim Affordable Housing Bonuses (Item 12, TC160005), granting administrative height, density (up to 75 units/acre), and zero-parking bonuses for transit-area projects reserving at least 15% of units for households at 60% AMI or below.

agenda_items.title: Pledge by Troop 451, Roll Call, and Consent Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel called the meeting to order, Troop 451 led the Pledge of Allegiance, and all seven council members were present. With no priority items, Council approved the consent agenda 7-0, covering the Cross Connection Control audit, transportation and Durham-Orange County transit grant ordinances, Birchwood Park and American Tobacco Trail parking construction, and South Ellerbe stormwater demolition.

agenda_items.title: Amendment to City Noise Ordinance Section 26-23 (Durham Central Park)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Attorney presented a noise ordinance amendment addressing complaints from Liberty Warehouse residents regarding rehearsals in Durham Central Park by the samba-reggae group Batalá Durham, proposing an exemption between 10:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. Batalá Durham representative Mr. Anderson welcomed clear rules and asked Council to consider other city parks as well, while Charlie Reece noted broader complaint-driven enforcement concerns were referred to the Environmental Affairs Board. Reece moved to extend the Central Park exemption window from 8:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m., which passed 7-0, followed by 7-0 adoption of the amended ordinance.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment TC170005 (Omnibus 11 Technical Revisions)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Michael Stock presented Omnibus 11 (TC170005), containing technical corrections, reorganizations, and minor policy codifications across the UDO (recommended 13-0 by Planning Commission). With no public speakers, Council adopted the consistency statement and ordinance amendment 7-0.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment TC170006 (Sedimentation, Erosion Control, and State Legislation)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Michael Stock presented TC170006 updating UDO subdivision exemptions, infrastructure performance guarantees, and sedimentation/erosion control rules to comply with North Carolina session laws (SL 2017-10, 2015-187, and 2017-40), approved 13-0 by Planning Commission. Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson and Mayor Schewel noted for the public that state legislative preemption was forcing Durham to weaken local environmental and development protections. Council adopted both motions 7-0.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment TC160005: Compact Neighborhood Interim Affordable Housing Bonuses
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Hannah Jacobson presented TC160005 offering administrative density bonuses (up to 75 units/acre), height bonuses (up to 90 feet), and zero minimum parking in Compact Neighborhood light-rail transit tiers for walkable projects reserving at least 15% of units for households earning 60% AMI or less (tightened from 70% AMI average after work session feedback, consistent with Council's 2015 resolution). Affordable housing advocates praised linking zoning bonuses to 60% AMI affordability for the first time, while Council Member DeDreana Freeman and others discussed transit-station outreach and whether developers would utilize the bonuses. Council adopted the consistency statement and ordinance 7-0.

votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved amending Section 26-23(e)(7) to extend Durham Central Park's permitted sound window from 10:00 a.m.–8:00 p.m. to 10:00 a.m.–9:00 p.m.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Feb. 5, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: All seven members of the Durham City Council convened on February 5, 2018, opening with Mayor Steve Schewel's State of the City address—which highlighted participatory budgeting, $80 million in 2018 affordable housing investments, light-rail transit, police racial-equity reforms, and a food security coordinator—alongside a Human Relations Month proclamation. Council unanimously approved the consent agenda (excluding pulled Item 13) 7-0, and approved both the Copley Farm rezoning for 123 residential units (Item 15, 2 votes) and the Angier Avenue consolidated annexation and rezoning for 78 single-family homes (Item 16, 3 votes) 7-0. On pulled Consent Item 13 (city code and fee revisions for small wireless 5G facilities under House Bill 310), Council split 4-3 to adopt the ordinance immediately over AT&T's request for a two-week delay: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved immediate adoption, while Steve Schewel explicitly announced he was voting Nay to grant a two-week delay and DeDreana Freeman voiced opposition regarding HB 310 preemption and delaying two weeks (individual names of the remaining voters were not read aloud on the record).

agenda_items.title: Mayor's State of the City Address, Neighbor Spotlight, and Human Relations Month Proclamation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel delivered his State of the City address outlining priorities including planning for participatory budgeting, $80 million in 2018 affordable housing efforts backed by Durham's dedicated two-cent housing tax levy, the $2.5 billion Durham-Orange Light Rail project, police reforms under Chief Davis (44% drop in car searches and misdemeanor diversion), and funding a food security coordinator. Council also presented a Neighbor Spotlight and proclaimed February 2018 as Human Relations Month honoring the Human Relations Commission's 50-year legacy.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval (Excluding Pulled Item 13)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With Item 13 (small wireless facilities) pulled for separate consideration, Council unanimously approved the consent agenda 7-0, including sidewalk construction administration contracts for Avondale and Campus Walk and a Campus Walk NCDOT supplemental agreement.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change for Copley Farm (365 Freeman Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jacob Wiggins presented Lennar Homes' request to rezone 30 acres at 365 Freeman Road from Residential Rural to PDR 3.997 for up to 123 single-family, townhome, or semi-attached units with 24% maximum impervious surface (Planning Commission approved 13-0). Robert Schunk highlighted a $22,000 DPS school proffer and a Southern High School trades-program partnership, while Mayor Schewel urged developers to also develop affordable housing fund contributions for suburban developments. Council adopted the consistency statement and zoning ordinance 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation for Angier Avenue Residential (3838–3848 Angier Avenue)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jamie Sunyak presented Angier Development LLC's voluntary annexation, utility extension agreement, and rezoning from RS-20 and PDR 4.0 to PDR 3.958 for up to 78 single-family homes across 19.96 acres on Angier Avenue (Planning Commission approved 13-1). DeDreana Freeman commended developer David Lazo for holding a late-evening neighborhood meeting with residents. Council adopted the annexation, consistency statement, and zoning ordinance 7-0.

agenda_items.title: City Code and Fee Ordinance Revisions for Small Wireless Facilities (Pulled from Consent)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: AT&T representative Robert Deroc requested a two-week delay on the small wireless (5G) ordinance to discuss potential discrepancies with NC House Bill 310 privately with staff. Public Works' Daniel Valero and the City Attorney confirmed the draft complied with HB 310 and noted permit applications were already arriving; Mark-Anthony Middleton rejected delaying for private offline talks after the work-session review, while DeDreana Freeman raised concerns over HB 310 pre-empting municipal right-of-way fees and Mayor Schewel favored granting a two-week grace period. Middleton moved immediate adoption, passing 4-3 with Mayor Schewel explicitly voting No on the record.

votes.discussion_detail: Adopted voluntary annexation effective March 31, 2018 and utility extension agreement for 3838–3848 Angier Avenue.

votes.discussion_detail: Adopted statutory consistency statement for Angier Avenue Residential.

votes.discussion_detail: Approved PDR 3.958 rezoning permitting up to 78 single-family homes along Angier Avenue.

votes.item_title: Item 13: Adopt City Code and Fee Ordinance Revisions for Small Wireless Facilities
votes.notes: Transcript announces 'Motion passes 4-3' without reading individual electronic votes aloud; Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and spoke in favor, Steve Schewel explicitly announced voting against, and DeDreana Freeman spoke critically of HB 310 and asked about a two-week delay.
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved immediate adoption of the HB 310 small wireless facilities code and fee ordinance, while Steve Schewel announced his No vote to grant AT&T a two-week delay; motion passed 4-3.

disagreements.issue: Immediate Adoption vs. Two-Week Delay on Small Wireless Facilities (5G) Ordinance (Item 13)
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-3 on adopting the small wireless facilities code and fee ordinance immediately versus delaying two weeks after AT&T requested additional time to review House Bill 310 compliance with staff.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt the ordinance immediately and adjust later if needed
side_a_arguments: Public Works staff had already built the permit workflow and were actively receiving 5G small-cell applications without codified local authority
Mark-Anthony Middleton argued the item was vetted at work session, other utilities did not object, and Council should not pause for private offline negotiations
disagreements.side_b_position: Delay action two weeks for stakeholder feedback or oppose HB 310 restrictions
side_b_arguments: Steve Schewel voted No to grant AT&T two weeks of grace so utilities could review the published text
DeDreana Freeman questioned any harm from a two-week delay and raised concerns over HB 310 stripping municipal fee authority over public rights-of-way
disagreements.resolution: Ordinance passed 4-3, with City Manager Tom Bonfield and staff committing to meet with AT&T and bring back any needed amendments.
